speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that internal bickering by Hockey Canada and the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association has caused postponement of the scheduled Canada Cup series this fall, and because this announcement comes on the heels of the impressive Soviet victory over the NHL, thereby creating a somewhat non-sportsmanlike impression around the world, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That this House not only compliment the Soviets for their brilliant Challenge Cup Victory, but instruct the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) to take all necessary action in resolving the differences between the two hockey bodies which fall within her jurisdiction, namely, Hockey Canada and the CAHA, in order to give Canadians the opportunity to recreate the emotional and unifying Canada Cup series of the past, as scheduled.

subsubtopic: CLARIFICATION OF STATEMENTS BY VARIOUS MINISTERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of statements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) which warned that the loss of Quebec would spell the loss of Canada, and considering the contradictory nature of those statements when compared to recent remarks by the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid) and the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. De Bane) whose comments suggested that if a strong majority of Quebeckers voted for separation, the Liberals would have no choice but to let Quebec go, which again appear diametrically opposed to remarks by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) who said that the government would not negotiate sovereignty association, I move, seconded by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse):
That this House direct the government to clarify these contradictory statements by various ministers which breed uncertainty and lend legitimacy to the separatist cause in Quebec.

In view of the fact that right now the Canadian Wheat Board is obtaining for farmers 58.5 cents per bushel more for barley, and 65 cents per bushel more for feed wheat, than the private enterprise open market, and in view of the fact that if all domestic feed grains had been handled by the board during the first four months of this crop year, $60 million more would have been put into the pockets of prairie farmers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT BANK OF CANADA BE AUTHORIZED TO LEND MONEY TO PROVINCES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an extremely urgent motion of pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the Government of Canada has obtained from a syndicate of American and European banks a credit margin of $3.5 billion whose security is based on the productive capacity of Canadians and considering that such financing operations in the public sector make our debt heavier from year to year, something which cannot go on without dangerously affecting our national economy and prosperity and jeopardizing the survival of generations for whom we are now sacrificing ourselves, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That, as a solution to that serious problem, the Minister of Finance introduce in the House a bill aimed at amending the Bank of Canada Act to enable it to grant long-term loans to federal and provincial governments, such loans being based on the real credit of the country, as is the case for the security of loans granted by chartered banks in Canada and by foreign banks, but whose excessive interest rate is burdening the country for generations to come and compelling Canadians to reimburse $5 in capital and interest for each $1 borrowed, and that those loans be granted at a rate equivalent to administration costs.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FAULTY WORKMANSHIP UNDER AHOP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs with respect to some of his domestic responsibilities.
Earlier in this House, under repeated questioning with respect to faulty inspections and the use of inadequate building materials in AHOP projects-specifically under the AHOP project at Virginia Park in St. John's-the minister said many times that CMHC is only responsible for inspections to ensure construction process for mortgage purposes. Yet, according to a confidential document prepared for the minister and CMHC, this statement is made:
Provision of insurance entails appraisal and inspection of units and this served to provide a kind of guarantee to purchasers on the quality and workmanship of these units.
I ask the minister if this assurance to the purchasers on quality and workmanship with respect to AHOP units applies to the unfortunate people who bought AHOP houses in Virginia Park and now find they have depreciated in value because of deteriorating brick and inadequate inspection.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FAULTY WORKMANSHIP UNDER AHOP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in relation to the people who live in Virginia Park, an offer has been made to them in an amount sufficient to repair deficiencies. These disbursements will be made as repairs are carried out.
The increase in the monthly payment which will eventually occur will be delayed for a number of months to make it easier for these borrowers to repay the amount. Therefore, the net increase in monthly payments will be postponed until the end of the first five-year loan. With regard to these people, a concrete offer has been made to help solve their problems.

subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FAULTY WORKMANSHIP UNDER AHOP
speechtext:
The minister is all heart, Mr. Speaker. These people have, rightly, declined that offer because on a house that has depreciated in value their liability would increase by increasing the mortgage. Therefore, they turned it down.
Virginia Park is merely the tip of the iceberg: we know of other faulty inspections and faulty materials being used in AHOP projects across the country. The minister will have to face up to this sooner or later. People in Virginia Park, through their solicitor, have rightly declined this offer which would merely add to their liability.
What are the minister and the department prepared to do for the people who bought these houses through CMHC in good faith, with the assurance they had had adequate inspection? The houses have now deteriorated because of inadequate inspection and because of faulty brick. We know there is an

investigation under way into allegations of pay-offs respecting CMHC inspectors. What is the minister going to do for these people. Why does he not tell us now, instead of giving us all this rhetoric?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FAULTY WORKMANSHIP UNDER AHOP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are basic errors in the remarks of the hon. member, which was not a question at all. First, he stated that these houses had been bought through CMHC. That is absolutely untrue. Second, he said there has been wrongdoing by some officials of CMHC. I think he is too quick in his conclusion. The investigation is not complete. Everyone should have the opportunity of a fair trial before being condemned, and not as the hon. member is trying to imply. Third, the hon. member gives the impression that this is only the tip of the iceberg.
During the last 15 years, housing worth millions of dollars has been built under guarantee by CMHC. This program has been a success all over Canada. Because there is a small problem in one project, we should not do as the hon. member is trying to do and create the impression that these homes built with the assistance of CMHC are bad and our program should be reprehended.

subtopic: RATE AT WHICH CANADA OBTAINED LOAN OF $3 BILLION FROM AMERICAN AND EUROPEAN BANKS
RATE AT WHICH CANADA OBTAINED LOAN OF $3 BILLION FROM AMERICAN AND EUROPEAN BANKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who has now become the most important minister in light of the present economic situation of Canada. Could he tell the House the rate of interest on the loan of more than $3 billion Canada has obtained from an American or European bank consortium and against what collaterals did the country obtain such a credit margin?

subtopic: RATE AT WHICH CANADA OBTAINED LOAN OF $3 BILLION FROM AMERICAN AND EUROPEAN BANKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have obtained that $3 billion credit margin from two groups. First from a Canadian group, but in American dollars, second from international banks under the leadership of an American bank. We obtained those loans by accepting to pay a certain rate of interest to maintain that credit margin, a rate I mentioned several times in the House. I do not have it here but I could provide it to the hon. member along with the collaterals we have given to our creditors. These of course are always the same, that is to say the country itself. That is the very best guaranty we can offer. Canada's credit is excellent everywhere in the world.

subtopic: RATE AT WHICH CANADA OBTAINED LOAN OF $3 BILLION FROM AMERICAN AND EUROPEAN BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. The minister has just given a formidable reply, except that he forgot to mention the interest rate, and Canadians will certainly wonder whether it is 10, 9 or 8 per cent. ter, has obtained a credit margin of several hundred million dollars, could the minister indicate to the House whether this credit margin from the same banks, from the same American or European consortium, has been granted with the same guarantees which the minister has just spelled out.

CHAIRMANSHIP OF NATIONAL FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Knowing the minister's opposition to anyone outside the immediate farm community playing a prominent role in farm policy decisions, was it the minister's own decision to remove Mr. Paul Babey from the chairmanship of the National Farm Products Marketing Council and to replace him by Mrs. June Menzies, formerly of the Anti-Inflation Board, and is this part of the government's over-all food strategy proposals?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CHAIRMANSHIP OF NATIONAL FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the things we said we would do was put people from other parts of society on the National Farm Products Marketing Council. Mrs. June Menzies is from the province of Manitoba, another part of Canada. She has knowledge both of agriculture and of the consumer sector. I had a meeting with Mrs. Menzies this morning about the program of the National Farm Products Marketing Council.
Mr. Paul Babey, the former chairman of the National Farm Products Marketing Council, has a tremendous history of service to the rural community of Canada and to our whole society. He will make a tremendous contribution in the Farm Credit Corporation which is going through a reorganization at the present time. The knowledge Mr. Babey has will not be lost; it will be helpful to the agricultural industry in Canada and all around the world.

subtopic: CHAIRMANSHIP OF NATIONAL FARM PRODUCTS MARKETING COUNCIL

I am just saying that this organization will go ahead. It will be as healthy as the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency, which is one of the most successful marketing agencies in the world at this point. The cost of eggs has contributed less to the inflationary factor than the cost of nearly any other food we eat in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on the same subject, I have a question for the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, and I use the word loosely.
Since the Canadian Wheat Board has made a proposition that 10,000 new hopper cars have to be added to the grain fleet during the next six years, and the board says that unless these additions are made over and above the 2,000 cars they are purchasing with farmers' money, exports could decline by one million tons a year, which would represent a loss of over $4 billion in the western economy, and in view of the fact that the board has said that lack of railway cars is the number one problem affecting grain exports, what action does the government intend to take about this Wheat Board proposal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the hon. member can constantly turn what is a great story of progress into a pessimistic one. What we are talking about is expanding exports by one million to 1.5 million tonnes a year from a current record level of 21 million tonnes to a level of 30 million tonnes in 1985. That is what the cars are required for.
There is, of course, room for argument about whether by that time we will need 8,000, 9,000, 10,000 or 11,000 cars. But I want the hon. member to know that I immediately responded positively to the suggestion of the Wheat Board, and indeed I will be taking up the direct suggestion of the government of Saskatchewan that we set up a ministerial task force on the subject. It looks as though the messages from the premiers of Manitoba and Alberta may be read as being positive as well, provided we broaden the subject from just the hopper cars to the whole question of dealing with the over-all grain and transportation problem.
Certainly, at the Winnipeg meeting on January 8 and 9, all the premiers saw the facts. They emerged from that meeting positive that we could do the job of carrying this grain, exporting it and selling it, and that the important thing is confidence on the part of the producers so that they will produce it. So we will get that job done, Mr. Speaker.

Since it is not good enough for the minister to say we are doing as well as we did last year, and since the system is strained now, I should like to ask the minister whether or not he will implement the Hall commission recommendation for the Government of Canada to pay the difference between the Crowsnest or statutory grain rates and the compensatory rates, and require the railroads to purchase the rolling stock, hopper cars and locomotives, or anything else that is necessary, and save the money that he will spend on improving branch lines, save the money he is spending on branch line subsidies and on

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I find the logic of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre to be extraordinary. He suggests we should save the money we are spending on branch lines, save the money we are spending on hopper cars by giving the railways twice as much money, according to that suggestion of the Hall commission. What kind of logic that is, I do not know. At least the hon. member should not call it saving.
The fact of the matter is that the Hall commission has left us with a very serious dilemma still in relation to all of the products made from grain, and more and more people in the prairies are realizing that the discrepancy between freight rates on grain and freight rates on products, including meat, means they are at a disadvantage from the point of view of processing in the prairies. Indeed, studies which governments in the prairies have had commissioned have demonstrated this to them, although they have kept those studies secret. They have demonstrated that the prairies are being disadvantaged by this discrepancy, hence the suggestion by Mr. McMurtry- during an election campaign, it is true-that the province of Saskatchewan will be prepared to pay part of the cost in relation to products.
That is the issue which I will want to discuss further with him. I made the point to him that it seemed to me important that we solve the problem in the same way in Manitoba and Alberta as in Saskatchewan, but I was delighted that he recognized at this point-as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has never recognized-that the whole future of processing meat and products on the prairies depends on solving the whole problem, instead of responding to simplistic cries for giving the railways more money, thereby saving the money we are now giving the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: OIL SUPPLIES FROM MEXICO AND WESTERN CANADA TO EASTERN CANADA-GOVERNMENT PLANS

Mr. Speaker, Canadian supplies from western Canada have been increased recently under temporary arrangements. These Canadian supplies are displacing crude to the Chicago market; that is, crude which otherwise would have been supplied from offshore to the Chicago market. That crude is now going to eastern Canadian refineries. So, in fact, additional quantities of Canadian crude are being moved into eastern Canada through this exchange arrangement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FAMILY IN LIBERAL PARTY CAMPAIGN LITERATURE-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Order, please. Last Friday the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) gave notice of his intention to raise by way of a question of privilege a matter dealing with the printing of a document, which he then produced in the House, to determine first of all whether or not there was a question of privilege and, secondly, whether there was some responsibility in the administration of the House of Commons for the printing of the document. The hon. member followed up by giving me the text of a proposed motion which he would move in order that I could make a finding that the matter on a preliminary basis did touch the privileges of a member. His draft motion is as follows:
That the publication by the Liberal party of the pamphlet entitled "Parliamentary Report" be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections with instructions that the said standing committee study the format and subject matter of the said pamphlet and report back to the House as to whether the said pamphlet offends the office of the Governor General according to traditional usage and custom.
According to the hon. member's remarks on Friday, matter in question appeared to be election material used by the Liberal party and containing a picture of the Governor General and his wife. In addition, the hon. member indicated that this would appear to be a blatant misuse of the office of the Governor General. The hon. member asked whether the printing of the document was done by the House of Commons facilities or whether it was authorized by me, and if not, by whom.
I can dispose immediately of the matter as a proposed question of privilege. It has been said time and time again that the law of parliamentary privilege is restrictive in nature in that it consists in the main of rights which are necessary for the execution of the powers of parliament, that privileges are enjoyed by individual members in order that members may carry on their functions in an unimpeded way. In order to constitute interference with that privilege, there has to be an obstruction of the basic ability of a member to perform those duties or, alternatively, there has to be some kind of contempt.
Whatever else it may be, it is clear to me that the production and circulation of this particular document would not appear to constitute a breach of parliamentary privilege as such.
That having been said, the hon. member also asked me to determine the authorization for the printing of the document

and interesting and important questions with respect to the provision of services by the House of Commons raised by this matter, in that the production of what we refer to as householder mailings is carried on as a service of the House to its members. I think all hon. members understand that this is a service to them to be taken advantage of up to four times a year in order that the member may provide information to his constituents, constituents of all political persuasions, about the events taking place here in parliament.
Bearing in mind that the function is informational in nature, that it is for constituents of all political persuasions and that it is provided not at party expense but at public expense through the estimates of parliament, it is obvious that the document must have certain guidelines which fulfil the expectations of this kind of program. Indeed, these guidelines have been established, and I believe that most hon. members are familiar with them, although it has been some time since they have been discussed here in the House.
Perhaps it would be useful to repeat that there are restrictions with respect to the size of the document, the number of pages in each and the total number to be authorized over a fiscal year. I will not go into details, but those are some of the basic requirements set down in the guidelines available.
In general, under these criteria a householder mailing is acceptable, provided it does not include a text which (a) requests adhesion to a party, (b) invites constituents to attend national or constituency political meetings or functions, (c) requests monetary contributions, or (d) contains election campaign material including election speeches, poll activities and lists-in other words, material which is more specifically the responsibility of party or constituency headquarters.
These guidelines, which are reviewed from time to time, have been put in place after the most thorough consideration by the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services and, in general, seem to have fulfilled their purposes well. I do not need to remind hon. members that the membership of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services consists of members of all parties in the House.
There is a continuing consultation between the committee and the offices of hon. members on the one hand, the printing service on the other hand, and, of recent years, between the party research units and the printing units along the same lines. In that respect the practice of consultation between the party research units and the printing units in terms of doing something of a general nature which might be used to the advantage of an individual member or of a particular party is not an uncommon practice.
I have inspected the document referred to by the hon. member carefully. It is a proposed constituency mailing which begins with a photograph of His Excellency the Governor General and Her Excellency on the occasion of the installation of the Governor General, with a space for a photograph of the member sending the document. It is followed by a further photograph of His Excellency together with a short biograph-
February 12, 1979

ical sketch and some opinions concerning the proposed attitude to be taken by Elis Excellency on the question of national unity. The remainder of the proposed mailing is quite in accordance with the usual reports made by members to their constituents dealing with topics such as the federal-provincial conference, various committees of the House, the legislative proposals before parliament and so on.
I was interested to find that this is not the first occasion in which mailings by members have alluded to the office and person of the Governor General and of Her Majesty the Queen.
The question I have to determine is whether or not the proposed mailing is in contravention of the guidelines as they exist at the present time. In my opinion, it is not. By definition, parliament is composed of the Governor General, the Senate and the House of Commons, and it would seem to me therefore that the publication is in essence parliamentary in nature. It seems to me, on inquiry, that the official in the printing unit who did not feel that the proposed publication contravened the established guidelines which would have resulted in his bringing the document to the attention of his superiors was acting within the guidelines as he understood them, and as I understand them.
As I have previously said, these guidelines, which have been most helpful to hon. members, are in existence as a result of careful consultation with the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services. The committee may, in its wisdom, wish to consider the guidelines again and be more restrictive, if that is their desire; but for the time being I must tell the hon. member that, according to the criteria now in force, the mailing is acceptable.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Buchanan that Bill C-12, to amend the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act and the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I got to my feet in this debate Thursday night, there were only about ten minutes left so I was not able to do much more than make some introductory remarks. I hope that even in those remarks I made it clear that we feel very strongly that the principle of the indexation of pensions is sound. We are glad that we have won the implementation of that principle, at least to some extent. We hope the day will come when it will apply to all pensions, both in the public and in the private sector.
So far as the public sector is concerned, we have full indexation of old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, other pension programs such as the Canada Pension Plan, the disability pension that is paid to war veterans, and the war veterans allowance. We also have it with respect to the family allowance, even though we lost some of the indexation when in January of this year the basic family allowance payment was put back to $20.
The fact is that we have a fair amount of indexation of pensions that are available, if they meet the conditions, to all the people of Canada. The indexing of pensions of retired public servants, retired personnel of the Canadian Armed Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and so on, is not the only example of indexing of pensions in the public sector.
As I say, we take very strongly the position not only that indexing of pensions is sound, but that, without indexing, pensions are not really pensions. What point is there to a person being given a certain amount to live on at the time of his retirement if the amount has to stay at that level no matter what happens to the cost of living? In the course of a few years, a pension that is not indexed can become no pension at all.
I urge very strongly that the direction in which we should be moving should not be to respond to the campaign that wants to cut out the indexing of public service pensions. We should be moving in the direction of finding ways to guarantee that the pensions of all Canadians, whether they are public or private, are subject to indexation.
As I said the other evening, another direction in which we should be moving is that of making indexation something that

is related not just to the rise in the cost of living but to the rise in the standard of living. It is my view that it is not good enough to say to a person who has retired that he will get enough money to buy for the rest of his years the basket of goods and services he can buy at that point, when everybody else in society is winning wage increases and an opportunity to share to some extent in the nation's increasing productivity.
I know that once we talk about pension indexing of that sort there are those who come back and ask us what it will cost. We are shown long advertisements and given long treatises on the amounts of money that are in various funds and so on. After the years that I have been studying and dealing with pensions, I have come to the conclusion that these funds are really a myth. After all, in most cases so-called pension funds are figures on pieces of paper. What really counts when pensions are being paid is the productiveness of the economy at the time those pensions are paid.
If you grant to a person a pension of $1 million a year and there is no economy producing goods and services in which that money is worth anything, the pension is worthless. Pensions are paid out of current production.
What we do in our whole scheme of pensions is to set up machinery whereby the part of the economy that is working produces enough for itself, for its children who have not yet gone to work and for the older people who have done their share of the work and have retired.
This attempt to fall back on myths about funds is a false view of the whole thing. What we should be concerned about is the fact that it is our responsibility as a society not only to provide for the retirement years of all our people, but to provide for that retirement on a basis that will enable them not just to keep up with the cost of living, but to continue to share in the rising standard of living.
I used the phrase the other night that I wanted all Canadians to be part of the Canadian family. In any family situation, you do not distinguish between the different members of that family by age or any other characteristic. You do as well as you can with what you have for all the members of that family. We should do as well as we can for all members of the Canadian family. That means that our retired people are entitled not only to pensions, but to have those pensions escalated to enable them to share in the growing productivity which, after all, they helped to make possible through their years of work.
We are proud of the role we have played-and I had something to say about this in a reflective mood the other night-in getting the escalation of various kinds of pensions established. We decry as strongly as we can the campaign that some are waging to try and turn back the clock.
Having said that, may I make a few comments about the bill before us. In so doing, I should like to deal with some of its specific provisions. I begin by saying I would be happy if the bill were not before us at all; I would be quite happy if we continued with the present plan which calls for full indexing of
February 12, 1979

the various pensions covered by the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. However, there has been a vicious campaign and many people have been taken in by arguments that certain individuals are being favoured as opposed to others. So there is a campaign to do something. This bill is an attempt on the part of the government to answer that criticism, to retain the principle of indexation as applied to the pensions of all those covered by the plans under the aegis of the government, and yet to relate the payments in some way to the figures on the books which correspond to what persons have contributed out of their wages and salaries toward their retirement. In the light of that campaign which has gone on, I think the bill has to be described as one which it would be reasonable for us to accept.
There are some changes I should like to see made and there are some comments I wish to make during the committee stage, but one of the reasons 1 accept this measure is the suspicion that, if we fail to do so, then down the road we might get something worse. So we had better grab while we can a way of preserving the principle of indexation even if it means a slight reduction of the amount which some of those in the upper reaches of the public service are able to enjoy.
The bill covers three main areas affecting pensions of public servants, armed forces personnel and retired RCMP personnel, but perhaps I might say before going into this aspect that the other provisions in the bill are quite acceptable. I refer to the part of the bill which sets up pension arrangements for air traffic controllers and to the clauses which iron out a few technicalities in the Supplementary Benefits Retirement Act and related pieces of legislation.
Now to get to the three main things which the bill does with regard to pensions covered by the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. They are, first, a change with respect to the amount of indexation one gets in the first January of his retirement. Then there is something with respect to those who are able to retire at age 55 after 30 years of service; and then there is the triennial scheme which is at the heart of this proposal.
As far as the change to a monthly or pro rata basis for the first pension indexation is concerned, I think this has to be regarded as reasonable. I know that some of the public service organizations which have produced briefs in connection with this bill have objected even to that. I read the briefs closely to see what those objections were. One was along the line that there are shortcomings in the plan as it is because pensions are based on a six-year average instead of three years or less, and that in a time of inflation retiring public servants do not get the amount of pension they should enjoy. In these circumstances it is argued that the ability to retire in October, November of December and benefit from indexation in January makes up for some of the shortfall they have suffered.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be far better to correct the mistakes and make changes where the amount of the pension itself is not good enough than to continue with a system which seems to involve a degree of unfairness as between employees who retire at different times during the year. I am certainly prepared to listen to those who want to
Pensions
argue against such a change, but on the face of it I think it must be said there is some argument in favour of it. The proposal is that persons who retired during the latter part of the year should get indexation in January on a pro rata basis in respect of the number of months they have worked in that last years. That seems reasonable.
The second thing this bill does raises some complications. A few years ago a provision was made that if a person was 55 years of age and had 30 years' service he could not only retire but could get immediate indexation. We understand, of course, that people can retire early under other conditions as well. The provision to which I have just referred has been in effect for a few years and there have been some rather notorious cases. I shall not put names on record; some of those names are too well-known. However, a few favoured persons with 30 years' service have been able to retire, get immediate indexation and then go straight off to other jobs.
It is to correct this abuse that the government has decided that from now on indexation will begin only at age 60. Even that statement has to be qualified. Persons already getting indexation at an earlier age will continue to receive it and people who would be getting it during the next year or so will be covered by a notch formula. It is still true, and will be true, that persons retired for medical reasons will receive indexation right away, as will widows of pensioners even though the person getting the pension is under 60. Nevertheless, public servants generally will not have the right which a few already enjoy. There were abuses there and it is not unreasonable for the government to take account of them and to correct them.
At the time we brought in this provision for retirement at age 55 after 30 years of service I had a good deal to say about the position of retired members of the RCMP and the Canadian armed forces. Though the same rule applied to them, many retired personnel from these two groups had not completed 30 years of service; retirement in their case was not voluntary, they were under contracts which made it necessary for them to retire, some of them as young as 49 or 50. So there was no possibility of their getting indexation until they had reached the age of 60.
I have argued for several years now that, it having been made possible for some top public servants to get indexation at 55, at least we ought to make the same thing possible for retiring RCMP and CAF personnel, especially if they are retiring involuntarily or because of the nature of their contract. I suppose there will be some hon. members opposite who will say that now that we have taken away the right of top public servants to retire at 55 and get immediate indexation, that ends the argument about RCMP and Canadian armed forces personnel.
I do not think it ends the argument at all. I think it still stands, and one of the things I want to look very hard at when we get into committee on the bill is this whole business with respect to persons who I think have a claim to early indexation. Let us not in the process of getting rid of one abuse create

February 12, 1979
Pensions
another piece of injustice. As I say, I plead the right of these people to be considered. If we do have delegations before the committee, I am sure there will be delegations representing the armed forces and the RCMP, and I hope we will listen very attentively to their case.
I now move on to the main subject of the change with regard to public service pensions, and that is this triennial scheme which is being proposed. The way it stands now, it is a full indexation guaranteed and automatic for life for everyone once it starts, but the new proposal is that every third fall there should be an assessment of how much money is on the books, not in the fund. There is no fund. There are just figures out there on the books, but how much is there, how much of it really belongs to pensioners who are out of the service and out there enjoying their retirement, how much interest is that money earning and how much extra interest is it earning because we are in a time of high interest rates and so forth? A calculation is to be made each third fall as to how much could be charged against the books in the next three years, and on that basis what pensions will be paid.
We are told that had this bill come into effect at the beginning of 1979, the calculations last fall were such that there would have been a guarantee of the first $7,000 of everyone's pension being fully escalated but that the amount in excess of $7,000 would be escalated at 8 per cent this year, 7 per cent next year and 6 per cent in 1981.
I welcome the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) the other night that conditions have altered a bit since last fall, and he says it is likely that when that kind of assessment is made this fall for the years 1980, 1981 and 1982, those who do the calculating may be able to do a little better. I think he said, for example, that what might happen is that the threshold might be $7,500 or $8,000. I hope it will be, and I hope that if the figures are better that is how it will be applied, and rather than a higher rate of interest on the upper increments of pension it will be applied to raise that threshold.
That is the scheme which is being proposed, and I wish the bill were not before us at all. I would rather leave it exactly as it is, but rather than run the risk of some drastic change in the whole scheme I would say that this bill is a protective piece of legislation and that on that basis it ought to be accepted. The other night the minister pointed out that if the estimates made every three years in the fall were too optimistic and too much money was paid out in the next three years, more than should have been, then that would be corrected the next time around.
I asked about the reverse situation, supposing there was too pessimistic an estimate, and the minister gave me an acceptable answer to the effect that if not enough was paid out in a three-year period, that would mean there would be more money on the books-let us not talk about funds; we know there are no funds around at all-and that it would be possible to pay better pensions later on. I am accepting all of this as a piece of protective legislation, and I hope public servants will see it that way.

By the way, we have been told that the scheme which would have come into effect this year-something like that which will come in next year-would have covered about 60 per cent or more of the retired public servants themselves and about 90 per cent or more of the survivors and those who are out on disability pensions. Of course, the reason it is 90 per cent in the latter case as opposed to 60 per cent in the other case is that those pensions are that much smaller. But we are talking about an arrangement under which pensions of $7,000- perhaps $7,500 or $8,000-are protected with full indexation, and I am glad that that is true. Let it also be clear that the person who has a pension of $10,000 will get full escalation on the first $7,000, but then a little less escalation on the portion above that amount.
I am talking about all these figures and calculations, this triennial business and so forth, as though I regard them as fully valid, and no doubt before this debate is over figures in the millions, billions and trillions will be cited as though something really sacred attaches to them. We are moving on. When I first came here we talked of $500 million as though it was a terrific sum of money. Now we are getting into trillions.
I think these funds and these accounts are all a myth. I remember seeing in Hansard where C. A. Dunning told J. S. Woodsworth that we could not afford to pay a pension of $20 a month to our old people because it would break the country. But what are we doing now? Some would say we are breaking the country now. Not at all, as far as I am concerned. By providing these things we have made the country. I suggest that if we made up our minds that all our retired people on pensions of whatever kind were entitled to indexation, we could afford to do it out of current production. That is what we have to look at, not figures which are off in some musty books. What counts is the will to do it and the realization that we pay pensions out of current production because we believe our people are entitled to them.
One of the things I am hoping is that what we are now doing is simply going through a phase. It is a phase because, although we have indexation of public service pensions, old age security and the others I named a while ago, we do not have indexation of private pensions in the main but ought to. That day will come. Maybe there will have to be some sort of a tax element or government subsidy to make it possible, just as people pay into the supplementary retirement benefits account for public service pensions. Maybe there will have to be an account people pay into for the other, but I would say that the day will come when we will have extended the principle of indexing of pensions across the board. When that day comes we will be able to revise this triennial scheme which we have been forced to go into because of the kind of campaign we face, because of arguments about restraint and all the rest of it.
As I say, I wish the bill were not before us. I wish this triennial part were not proposed at all, but I think it is protective and has to be looked at favourably. I think we have to have hope and confidence that when we get beyond this
February 12, 1979

period and move into the protection of all pensions by proper indexing, we will put this one back on the full basis as well.
There are two or three other things I would like to say, and if my time is running out I hope that if I make the point that we do not have any other speaker for this debate today, the House will give me an extra minute or two if necessary.
One of the things 1 would like to speak about is a touchy subject which is thrown around, and that is the extent to which persons who want to kill the indexing of public service pensions talk about the pensions of members of parliament. We are accused of having had some complicity in the indexing of our pensions. This is always a touchy subject to deal with but I think it should be brought right out into the open.
No one in the House has any doubt where I stand on the subject of what we receive as pay and as pensions. I happen to think they are out of line with what we ought to be getting. I am not arguing that point at the moment, but I am establishing it as the basis for what 1 want to say. I think there are some things wrong with the pensions available to members of parliament. I think they are too generous. I object to the fact that the provisions for our widows are greater than for other widows. That is not fair. I also think the business of members of parliament being able to get a pension at any age once they have been here six years is preposterous, and I will come back to that in a moment. But the one thing in the members' pension plan that I think is not-

I thank you, sir, and I thank the House. I am afraid I put the House in a spot a moment ago, so that hon. members could not deny me extra time. What I want to say is that the one thing in the members' pension plan that I do not think is wrong is the business of indexing members' pensions, just the same as anyone else's pensions, provided that it starts only at the age of 60. Many people still have the notion that members' pensions are indexed as soon as the member of parliament leaves office. That indexing does not start until the age of 60.
As I said, I think there are things wrong with members' pensions that should be corrected, and I will indicate one or two of them right away, but that does not deny the right of members-just as I insist the right of public servants and elderly people, war veterans and people in the private sector- to have their pensions indexed in accordance with the rise in the cost of living. What we should be doing is to correct some of the things that are wrong.
The name of His Excellency the Governor General was dragged into debate a while ago in another context. I was pleased when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tabled some
Pensions
days ago copies of correspondence he has had with the Governor General, when he was just Mr. Schreyer, about his potential pension. Apparently the then Mr. Schreyer made the plea to the Prime Minister that he did not want to be in the position of being a retired Governor General at the age of 48 on full pension. He thought that instead that pension should be delayed until the age of 60. The Prime Minister's reply indicated that he was in agreement with that. He had some qualifications about disability or the possibility of his death and the leaving of a widow, but he agreed with the then Mr. Schreyer that it did not make sense for the Governor General to have a full pension at the age of 48 and that it should be deferred to the age of 60.
I think we should be doing that to our pension plan. If the Prime Minister is going to bring in legislation to correct the pension plan of the Governor General, 1 think we should correct this business of a member of parliament being able, once he has had six years of service, to draw a pension at any age.
There are a few other things which should be put closer into line with other pension plans, but it is these other things which stand to be corrected, not the right to pension indexation. I think that anyone, whether he is a member of parliament, a retired RCMP officer, a governor general or a CNR or CPR pensioner, if he is going to have a pension, should have one that would enable him to keep abreast of the rising cost of living and with the standard of living.
So, sir, I decry the kinds of attacks that have been made on the plans that are now in effect. But for the errors that I have just referred to in our own scheme, I think the plans generally are pretty good. There are a few things that are in the public service plan which should be corrected, and I am sorry they are not in the legislation before us now. A while ago I referred to the fact that the public service pension is based on the average of one's six best years. In a time of inflation that can rob a retiring public servant of a great deal of security. Certainly it should be reduced to three years or perhaps even fewer.
I raise again, as I have, not only for public servants but, especially for the RCMP and the armed forces personnel, the question of marriages which take place after one goes on pension. The present law in this respect is as archaic and outdated as it can be. If a woman marries a retired public servant or a retired army officer who has served his day and age, and he is in the 50s or approaching 60, she can be his wife for 20 years, he has paid into the fund, but there is no pension for his widow because he married after he became a pensioner. As I said, that situation should be corrected.
I have already referred to the case of indexing for RCMP and armed forces personnel in cases where they have to retire early because of the nature of their contract. I think also their particular superannuation acts should be corrected.
We still have left over the problems relating to the buying back of earlier service or the buying back of years spent in the armed forces. There are instances where this was made possible but the person affected could not afford it and passed it up,

and then at a later date wanted to buy back earlier service to improve his pension position but the cost had become prohibitive. I think that also should be corrected.
There are still a few old timers around who transferred from one pension plan to another more than 50 years ago. I do not mean they were pensioners then; they were public servants in those days. They call themselves the "old originals." They do not have the advantage of the modern arrangements that are in our pension plans. I think we should not be drawing these kinds of lines. When people are retired, older people who have served their country in the public service, in the armed forces, in the RCMP or in the private sector, they should not be treated differently depending upon the time when they came into the plan, the time they retired, or what-have-you.
So there are all these various improvements that should be made in the Public Service Superannuation Act, in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and in the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, and I hope we will make them. Perhaps I am asking the government to bite off too much between now and the end of this session, which has not many months to run, but that seems always to be the problem. Some of the things I have talked about, such as the six years' average, the late marriages, the buying back, and so on, have been talked about ever since I came here, and there is always some excuse why we cannot act on them. Sometimes the excuse is that the session is about over and it is time for an election. All right, some things are going to be done, if the session lasts long enough, and they are set out in this bill. We will have to look at them pretty closely, but I think these other things should be done as well.
With these comments, I say on behalf of my party that we are prepared to agree to the second reading of this bill so that it can be referred to the committee. Generally speaking, we approve of its tone because, as I said, it is a protective piece of legislation, protective in the sense that it keeps alive the principle of indexing of pensions. That is a principle which, in my view, must not only be kept alive but must be extended until it applies to all pensions in this country, whether in the public or the private sector.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not going to take part in this debate because I had been told that Bill C-12 should be referred to the committee as soon as possible. But I have only a few words to say since the previous speaker simply stated our agreement to have this bill referred to committee as soon as possible for further study as it concerns the indexing of early retirement pensions and the public service monthly rates.
With this bill, the government answers the criticisms of certain financial groups who have stated that the public service pension fund greatly exceeds that of private companies and that, in the long term, the cost of the program will exceed its revenue. Certain financial circles have progressively escalated

their fight to the death with the government on this issue since the end of 1976. This is a sensitive question because on the one hand, some of the arguments of the private sector seem justified while, on the other, the Public Service Allia'nce has achieved a master stroke by obtaining the cost of living indexation of pensions to protect the purchasing power of their members and retired employees. To a certain extent, Mr. Speaker, the bill aims at reducing the pressures exerted upon many private retirement programs for which the benefits are much inferior to those offered by the public service. Indeed, it is a recognized fact that the public sector generally supports pension plans in which the benefits are 9 per cent higher than those of the private sector.
The proposals of the government mainly affect three areas: early retirement, the monthly rate and indexation. They amend two different statutes: the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act and the Superannuation Act. The government wants to reduce progressively over a period of five years the age for early retirement. This amendment would affect mainly employees between 55 and 60 who have or wish to retire before the maximum eligible age. Of course, we believe that this must remain optional. Contributors must still have the option to do as they wish. As for the monthly rate, those who retire in January would receive eleven-twelfths of the authorized annual cost of living indexation adjustment. Those who retire in June would receive only half and those who retire in November would receive an automatic adjustment of one-twelfth of the inflation cost devaluation. At the present time, the person who retires receives the total amount of the indexation whatever the time of the year of his retirement.
At the limit, an individual could retire on December 31, 1977, for example, and on January 1, 1978 get the full indexing for the entire preceding year. Ad hoc indexing would allow the federal government to take automatic indexing out of the pension plan. The adjustments required as a result of the increase in the cost of living would from now on be made on an ad hoc basis. The public service pension board would set the indexing over a three-year period and in direct relationship with the amounts of money available in the government's pension funds. More specifically, the interests collected on pension funds would be distributed to eligible pensioners. Full indexing would take place only when the interests on the capital accumulated in the funds would be sufficient to cover the costs. As far as unions are concerned, all hon. members know their position.
Early retirement relieves more or less older federal employees who must retire for reasons of health. That is where one of the biggest problems lies. The new legislation would deny workers the right to compensation in the form of early pensions. It would also affect people who in this time of budget cuts are forced to take an early retirement because of our personnel cutbacks.
February 12, 1979

Indeed, we know very well that a person 57 years of age, for example, will have great difficulty finding a new job because of his or her advanced age compared with a younger person who still has several years of employment ahead of him or her. So for certain people early retirement becomes an insurance that will allow them to continue to receive a salary even if they find themselves out of a job because of our cutbacks. So we say that that policy includes benefits for the older worker while it is futile for younger individuals who usually find themselves another job sooner or later. So the act as it now stands takes care of employees who need it most, because those who get a new job, although they are now getting their pensions, would not benefit because the difference would be taken away by income tax.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the adjustment of pension plans according to age is a coming thing, and the government will have to move toward lower pension age, that is 60 for all Canadians. Later on this will come down to 55. However, the time is ripe in my view to realize that the pension age should be lowered to 60 for everyone. During the last election, we obtained help for pensioners' spouses. This is not enough this year in my view to clarify the situation for those who get married with old age pensions.
I hope that during studies on this subject the government will seriously consider alleviating the heavy burden on our shoulders, with a reduction of eligibility age to 60 for everyone, perhaps with help at 55 for spouses and normal pension at 60. Mr. Speaker, those were the few remarks I had to make. I hope we can refer the bill to committee as soon as possible.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the basic purpose of this bill is to make some change in the provisions for the indexing of pensions of public servants. It is true that the bill does some other things: it progressively increases the age at which full escalation can take place on retirement from 55 to 60, it reduces the incentive to retire on December 31 in each year, it makes some changes in the period of time over which the government must amortize deficiencies arising from general adjustments in salaries, and it does something with pensions for air traffic controllers. But I repeat, the main purpose of the bill is to deal with the indexing of pensions, and this is what I wish to speak about today.
As hon. members will know, 9 per cent of the people of Canada are retired. These people take up roughly 5 per cent of the national income. The only possible way that they may continue to get the same cut of the national pie is to have their purchasing power maintained, and that means that their pensions must be indexed. If the pensions are not indexed these retired people, people living on pensions, widows, orphans and dependants, are robbed a little each year.
The suggestion that indexing pensions to maintain the same purchasing power will bankrupt Canada is so ludicrous that one wonders how people of good sense could give it a second
Pensions
thought. I am not talking about increasing the pensions according to the standard of living. That point was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). For the moment I am talking about maintaining purchasing power. If there was any evidence that inflation led to a decrease in national income in real terms, there might be a case for such an idea, but the reverse is true. Even though there is inflation, there is real growth.
Canada's real growth for this year will probably exceed 4 per cent, and there is no reason to believe that we cannot adapt our policies in such a way that we can still live with inflation and have real growth. This has taken place in Brazil and a number of other countries for some time. It is an affront to the intelligence of the average human being to suggest that it will bankrupt the country if we try to maintain the purchasing power of people who are retired.
The public service superannuation plan was adopted over 40 years ago. At that time the actuaries made their usual assumptions about age of retirement, rates of interest, contribution rates expected as a result of life expectancy and so on. They assumed that the average earning rate for the plan would be 4 per cent, and I am sure that they assumed that the benefits paid would represent stable purchasing power. In retrospect, those assumptions turned out to be erroneous because the cost of living has eroded benefits paid out and interest earnings have escalated.
Let us look at the problems dealing with supplementation. In 1970 the supplementary benefits retirement fund was set up by an act of parliament in order to establish a separate fund to deal with escalation. The anticipated rate of escalation was 2 per cent per year. The employees would contribute one half of 1 per cent of their payroll and the employer would match it. That was subsequently raised to a contribution of 1 per cent by the employee and 1 per cent by the employer. It is quite clear that this fund, while adequate for a 2 per cent or 3 per cent inflationary increase, is not adequate for a 9 per cent, 10 per cent or 11 per cent rate of inflation.
It is no great exercise to attack this fund and say that it is bankrupt or inadequate, or to make other derogatory comments with regard to it. We must admit that the fund by itself is inadequate and cannot deal with the problem. But we must also look at what has happened to earnings. The earnings of the other fund are now approaching 8 per cent per year and rising. The average rate of interest is a weighted average of the long-term Government of Canada borrowings. The last borrowing by the Government of Canada had a nominal interest rate of 10>/4 per cent, and it was sold at a slight premium. The effective interest rate was in excess of 101/4 per cent. This means that the fund will continue to earn money at an even higher rate than was anticipated in the original calculation by the actuaries, which was 4 per cent. Indeed, this 4 per cent rate continued up until 1969. In the 1950s and 1960s the fund, in effect, was subsidizing the management of the public debt of Canada because it was an account in the books of Canada.

In response to a question I placed on the order paper, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) has filed some replies which were tabled in this House on October 10, 1978. I wanted to know the amount of money credited to the public service superannuation account as of March 31, and then I mentioned certain years. In 1965 it was $2,161 million. In 1970, the fund had grown to $3,600 million and in 1975 it had grown to $6,420 million. In March, 1976 there was $7,312 million in the fund and by 1977 it had $8,147 million. As of March 31, 1978 the fund had increased to $9,053 million and probably by March 1 of this year it will have exceeded $10 billion. That is an enormous sum of money.
There are those who say that the amount of money in the fund is negligible. I believe that the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan), who is alleged to be an expert in this area as an actuary, has a question on the order paper referring to the phantom funding. The public service superannuation account is an account in the books of Canada. It is part of the national debt. It is not generally recognized that the public service superannuation fund and the armed forces superannuation account together represent over one quarter of the entire gross public debt of the Government of Canada. It is reported in the public accounts and interest is accrued to it. I suppose that the hon. member who asked this question would have been much happier if the government had issued bonds, hired a clerk to clip the coupons and put them in the bank regularly once or twice per year. Somehow this would make him feel that he was meeting the test of actuarial soundness.
To me these sums of money are so large that what the government is doing with them is all that can be done. The hon. member for York-Scarborough has asked in one of his questions not yet answered whether the government has considered investing in the private sector. If the government put, for example, $10 billion into the private sector it would make Petro-Canada look like peanuts. Who would be the first to cry about socialism if we were to buy private equities? The official opposition. The simple truth is the sums of money are so large and the problems of debt management if these funds were diverted to some other use so great that the government of the day would have no alternative but to deal with the account as this government is doing now.
It is worth noting that, with a fund of $10 billion and a rate of interest which is credited at 8 per cent, the annual interest earnings on that fund are approximately $800 million. I put some questions on the order paper for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie)-

I recognize that an actuary can study the tables of life expectancy and mortality. I know actuaries have great skill and fine mathematical formulae. But when they project the rate of interest, not today but 25 years from now, 35, 45 years from now, may I suggest that that is not within their professional competence. When they have to project the rate of increase of wages in that period, they have no special claim to an expertise. When they have to project the rate of increase for the consumer price index, there is no special wisdom in their hands.
In making their projections and in stating that there was a $5.8 billion deficiency as of March 31st, 1978, they made the assumption that the average rate of inflation would be 6 per cent per cent, compounded, that the average rate of salary increase would be 8.5 per cent per year compounded, that the average rate of interest earnings would be 8.25 per cent compounded, and they assumed that the average retirement age would be 61.5 years. Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise here today to address one of the most emotional and misunderstood areas of government operations, amendments to the public service pension plans.
February 12, 1979

I referred deliberately to amendments to the public service plans in the plural because, as an actuary, I believe, along with the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), that the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act are merely separate parts of the whole. They must be viewed together to get a clear picture of what is happening.
For example, the changes proposed in Bill C-12 are only changes to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. However, I believe that if these changes are put into place a significant extra annual cost in the order of $100 million may be incurred under the Public Service Superannuation Act. The cost to the PSSA is not mentioned in the bill; it is hidden. That is why the actuaries and I who reported to the government in the spring on these plans urged that no change be made to either plan without examining the effects and cost of the change on both plans.
On all sides we, as members of parliament and as members of the public, are being bombarded with facts. Most of these facts are one-sided presentations of the actual situation. Many are downright misrepresentations of the actual situation. Indexed pensions are available to the Canadian public as a whole. Both the old age security and the Canada and Quebec Pension Plan payments are indexed for the cost of living. However, very few private pension plans are fully indexed. The actuarial survey tabled in parliament last spring indicated that only .6 per cent contained a full indexing provision. On the other hand, 80 per cent of the plans in the private sector have some form of post-retirement adjustments. These average 66 per cent of the change in the CPI.
It is obvious that if the public service is to be treated equitably in our society there must be provision for some indexing. However, we in parliament have two publics to represent, the general public and the public service. We have an obligation to see that the public service receives a first class pension, a pension that we can be proud of providing in recognition of service to the state. However, we also have an obligation to the general public to ensure that we do not create a preferred class in society, a class with benefits so far beyond what is available to the general public as to create serious social inequity.
Fully indexed pensions for civil servants were introduced in 1973. I must admit that in reading Hansard quite frankly I was amazed to find out that from introduction of the bill on first reading the royal assent of the bill took a grand total of ten days. On second glance, Mr. Speaker, this probably was not all that extraordinary because even though the then president of treasury board indicated that a contribution of "one-half of 1 per cent to go with the government's matching contribution will almost certainly be insufficient to cover the cost of escalation", there was a clear implication in his remarks that the cost was unlikely to be too much greater. 1 say there was a clear implication. I certainly would draw that conclusion from the remarks. However, a close reading shows
Pensions
the president of treasury board did not state that the funding was almost adequate.
Last April we had an estimate for the first time of what the indexing provision would cost. The indexing suggests that the employer contribution is of the order of 8.5 per cent of payroll. In other words, the initial contribution was one-seventeenth of what was required to be set aside. The original provision missed the mark by some 1,700 per cent.
We now know that in those ten days we approved measures which established an initial unfunded liability-that is, the cost of the benefits granted-of approximately $6 billion. The total budget for the Government of Canada in the fiscal year 1973-74 was $23 billion. In this one bill we spent the equivalent of one quarter of the total government spending in the year without seeing so much as an estimate or projection. I suggest that presenting a bill of this magnitude without any serious financial warnings was either dishonest or seriously negligent.
Public opposition to these pensions developed over several years and much criticism, informed and uninformed, was aired. In October, 1976, Treasury Board released the "Basic Facts" paper. The stated purpose of the "Basic Facts" paper was "to assess the retirement benefits of federal public servants ... To review how these benefits are financed and inform the House of Commons ... of some preliminary conclusions".
This document sought to establish both the reasonableness of benefit levels and the soundness of funding procedures. However, this "Basic Facts" paper contained several of those misrepresentations that I referred to. It stated that the impression that public service pensioners typically received pensions greatly exceeding those of most working Canadians was a misunderstanding. It stated that recent allegations that public servants live in a pension paradise are devoid of factual basis. It also stated that basic pensions are financed with the same actuarial principles which generally apply to private sector plans.
Actuaries are a wary breed. They are not easily excited. They are noted for their sang-froid. However, when that basic facts paper was published the Canadian Institute of Actuaries representing all actuaries in Canada, including all federal government actuaries, took an unprecedented step. It decided to issue an unsolicited public statement. If I may quote in part:
This document which was tabled ... purports to defend the public service pension system ... What is ironic is that the spuriousness or dubious validity of so many arguments ... aroused the suspicion or outright condemnation of practically every professional actuary who has examined the document.
We believe it is more constructive to address ourselves to two key questions.
1.	Is the system being properly financed?
2.	How do the benefits provided by the system compare with those of other Canadian employers?
No attempt is made to recognize the currently accruing cost of indexing ... In our opinion the value or cost of the indexing adjustments is systematically concealed and deferred for payment by future generations of taxpayers and public servants.
The benefits provided by the public service system ... are more generous (and in most cases much more generous) than those provided by ... private sector employers ... given a thorough ... understanding of these benefits ... Most

February 12, 1979
Pensions
private sector employees would be only too happy to contribute at a comparable rate if their employers would agree to provide comparable benefits.
In view of the furore created over this issue, the actuarial firm of Tomenson-Alexander was commissioned on March 23, 1977 by Treasury Board to determine the future cost implications, advise on the extent to which the compensation policy takes account of benefits under PSSA and SRBA, comment on the "Basic Facts" paper, assess other actuarial considerations and make recommendations regarding future actuarial investigations and reports. The report was sent to the then president of treasury board on November 30, 1977 and released on March 9, 1978, at which time several amendments to the act were indicated.
The report was very interesting. It indicated that no valuation of the plan had been made since December 31, 1972, before unlimited indexing was introduced. Not only had the government not found out what the plan was going to cost before they introduced it, but they had not found out what the plan was actually costing after they introduced it. This surely is the height of folly. If we are ever to convince the general public that public servants do not regard the public purse as virtually bottomless, as the Auditor General alleges, we must begin to subject ourselves at least to the rudimentary discipline of finding out what on earth these programs we have adopted cost or will cost.
The actuarial commission pointed out that the government was not funding its pensions in anything like the manner accepted in the private sector. In making comparisons with the private sector the government was even confusing the true cost incurred by the program with the smaller amounts that it was setting aside year by year.
In his introductory remarks to the House, the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) referred to the $490 million that the government is setting aside each year as the cost of these benefits. The point is that $490 million is not the true cost. They are not reporting the cost according to generally accepted accounting principles; that is the point. The government sets one set of rules for itself, rules that the private sector cannot possibly match, and then tries to pretend that the cost is much lower.
Another point in the initial address by the President of Treasury Board was that the government felt that private sector employers should be encouraged to introduce benefits along the same lines as public service pensions. If the private sector did that, it would have to conform to the rules of accounting for costs of pension plans available in the private sector. They would have to charge through an extra 10 to 20 per cent on salary. In other words, if they adopted these plans it would be equivalent to a 10 to 20 per cent salary increase on top of the regular salary increase.
A week ago we had the spectacle of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) hectoring the banks for giving bank tellers a total increase of 11.5 per cent. The President of the Treasury Board is suggesting they should get an additional 10 to 20 per cent on top of their normal increase to bring them up to the govern-

ment's level. Who is directing the economic policy of the country? On one hand we have people saying-
