He said: Mr. Speaker, in February 1978, I had the honour to command the attention of this House by introducing a motion dealing with the subject matter that has just been stated. That motion, like the one now under consideration, was intended to provide a means for increasing family incomes by paying an allowance or whatever to recognize the merits of our Canadian mothers and thus increase the total family income.
Mr. Speaker, 1 recall that the majority of members who had participated in the debate on this motion agreed on the principle. They recognized the rationale of the motion and none of the members had said anything against it or found a way to oppose to it. However, the solutions suggested to achieve that purpose were somewhat different. Mr. Speaker, if I am back this year with the same subject, it is because the problem has not been solved and because 12 months later, I am more convinced then ever that this parliament must make a financial effort to acknowledge that housewives in our country play a very important part not only within the family itself but within the community at large and also because they contribute to the increase in our gross national product. It is a fact we must acknowledge. Mr. Speaker, this year is the International Year of the Child. When there is a child, there is a mother. Sure, we must recognize the children's rights but mothers have rights too. Their rights are recognized in well-off families with an adequate income to meet the needs of each member of the family. But we cannot and should not separate the rights of the child from the rights of the mother.
My main concern, Mr. Speaker, lies with families whose income is inadequate to meet the needs of all their members, with families with income below the poverty line. Mr. Speaker, we must be consistent and honest with ourselves. A few years ago the Canadian parliament itself set up a Senate committee under the chairmanship of Senator Croll to study the situation of Canadian families, the poverty level, the lack of money in a country as prosperous as Canada blessed by God with enough natural resources of all kinds to meet the needs of all its inhabitants.
Mr. Speaker, in the report from the Senate committee, poverty is defined as follows, and I quote:
The time has come to stop blaming the mirror for not being a window-
The French translation of that quotation reminds me of the story of the ostrich which sees the storm coming but pretends there is no storm and puts its head in the sand until the storm is over. We, in parliament, are not ostriches, and we would like to take our responsibilities. The quotation continues:
The time has come to stop blaming the mirror for not being a window, for presenting us with things we would rather not see.
Obviously, everybody would like to see a higher level of confort for all. But all cannot be equally well off. Even the communists who preach the theory of economic equality do not have that. That is a fact. But as democrats, as people who believe in a distribution system which is as fair as possible, we should concentrate on helping those in the lowest income
Housewives' Allowance
brackets. We should make sure that at least the basic needs of the weakest in our society are met. So much the better if some people are better off. If my neighbour is well off while I am in dire straits, I can ask him for help. But let us least make sure the basic human needs are not. That must be our goal, and Canada can achieve it. The inquiry report said, and I quote:
The time has come for a little common honesty.
I believe that all together we are able to do that.
The poor, after all, are not poor of their own accord.
Of course, it must not be very funny! I was extremely poor once, and I was not so of my own accord. I accepted my situation because I had no choice. Like many of my fellow citizens, I experienced the depression years. Everybody remembers those extremely difficult years. It was far from pleasant. Since we did not know any better, we accepted our situation. But today, with all the media, with television which shows us all kinds of things, pleasant and less pleasant things as well as hateful things, everybody is well informed.
And further on:
The poor, after all, are not, as some still pretend, poor of their own accord. The poor have no uncommon moral flaw that sets them apart, let alone condemns them. They are casualties of the way we manage our economy and our society-and that fact is increasingly obvious to the poor themselves.
Mr. Speaker, there was a reason for spending money in trying to find out what the situation is and how to remedy it. So, in our society of 1979, we must do everything possible to discover the means to ensure poor families additional income and so enable them to live a bit more decently, without it impoverishing us collectively.
Last weekend-all the hon. members have seen similar cases I am sure-the head of a poor family came to my office to explain his situation. There are five of them in the family. The mother is sick; now sickness is not a fault; no one tries to be sick but when sickness comes it has to be accepted. And the father went on explaining how much medication costs him each month. Finally, I asked him what his income was. He works for an agency . . . now, what is it called ... a security agency. In any event, he earns $3.37 an hour. On the basis of a 30-hour week, how much income does that make? Deduct from that the pension plan and unemployment insurance contributions, and what have you left? About $122 a week. That is not much more than $6,000 a year.
It is easy therefore to understand how difficult it is for him to meet his obligations. His wife worked and still does as best she can. If the state, in an effort to distribute more equitably the gross national product, helped to raise the living standard of those families whose income is below the poverty line, if an attempt were made to grant those mothers some allowance that could supplement the income of the father who goes out to earn his family's keep we would be no worse off for it.

February 12, 1979
Housewives' Allowance
Last year, when this motion was discussed, one hon. member said: Well, listen here, if the hon. member wants to pay his wife a salary, it's okay by me. But it isn't up to the state to do so. To talk like that is to distort voluntarily the real meaning of the motion I had presented. Obviously, if I were president of a company and had a salary of $50,000 a year, I could pay $5,000 to my wife to help her look after her household duties, if I wanted to. However, this is not the situation of the unemployed, nor is it the situation of the welfare recipient. And they are in great numbers today, Mr. Speaker, in our society. The essence of the motion is purposely being clouded. What does the hon. member for Bellechasse intend to achieve with his motion? He simply wants to implement in our country the altogether practical idea of a minimum family income to ensure that each and every member of a given family has at least the opportunity to satisfy his or her fundamental needs.
Mr. Speaker, in the spring of 1978 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet introduced a measure to reduce the sales tax in order to help families with their budget and remove this burden of the sales tax on all items which are required in everyday life. Those were the arguments given by the Minister of Finance at the time. He submitted this was designed to exempt the largest families, those that consume most, from that sales tax burden in order to increase their net revenues. Second, it was meant to help this country's economy, because the increased purchasing power given to those families might boost consumption and thus allow our economy to perform at a more normal rate, through wider use of domestically produced goods. Such was the aim, to increase the purchasing power of individuals and families.
Mr. Speaker, last week I attended part of the first ministers' conference, between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the provincial premiers. There was a consensus, and I welcome this, that it was important for a new Canadian constitution to include in the first chapter the rights of individuals and families. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the individual is entitled to sufficient revenues from work and other sources where he is unable to support himself. The same thing goes for families, Mr. Speaker. Families are the cornerstone of our society, the basic cell created by the Lord, because as I said if it were man's invention it would have long since disappeared.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the name of Canadian mothers who really contributed and are now contributing to this country's development by giving our society boys and girls to fill important functions, I say we have an obligation, a duty to them, and I feel this is the time to try and show them that we, as managers of this country's affairs, recognize their important role in our society through economic and financial provisions.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing to support alternative measures if they fulfil that objective. But my insistence is that we make an effort to compensate for the purchasing power lacking in families at or below the poverty line.

As I said, Mr. Speaker, whether she be poor or a millionaire, the mother giving birth to a child contributes just the same. She puts the same effort and deserves the same recognition. If the millionaire mother has advantages, so much the better. But we as legislators should strive to compensate for the low income of families where the provider earns a mere pittance, or is unemployed.
Heaven knows if there are jobless now in this country. I do not want to blame anyone but I say that today it is disappointing for mothers who made sacrifices to enable their young daughters to attend high school, the CEGEP or university so that they may earn a decent living, when those young girls- and it must be the same thing for everyone in this House- when those young girls after completing their education apply to an employer with their diploma, whether in the federal government or the provincial government or in the private sector, and they are asked: Do you have any experience? Since the young girl has just finished school, she can only answer: No, sir, I do not have any experience but I am willing to try. The employer tells her: We only hire experienced people here. Those young girls make their way back home and tell father or mother: It's too bad, he would have hired me, but I have no experience.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like the government, the Parliament of Canada, to be aware enough of those situations- there are hundreds of them-I would not want my words to be distorted-to allow those mothers who voluntarily want to stay home, because their role is to stay there, not to be penalized, not to be punished for choosing that role as opposed to those who decided to go and work in industry, in business or elsewhere. We now have in the province of Quebec-I say so because I know what I am talking about-young girls, registered nurses, who are refused jobs because other people without a degree are being hired to do the same work for less. I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are about to tell me that my time is up.
I would have had so much to say in favour of mothers, but I want all mothers in Canada to understand that I wanted by my motion to show them that they are performing an important role in this country and that we have a duty to them. I urge all my colleagues in the House to consider that we should fulfil our obligations to them by recognizing a right-the right to a decent family income.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR THE PAYMENT OF A HOUSEWIVES' ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to extend the customary commendation to the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for bringing forward motion No. 15 respecting the payment of an allowance to housewives. Unfortunately, I cannot support the motion, although certainly I support the principle, as I am sure all members of the House do, of assisting families to meet spending needs which result from the presence of children within the family unit. I believe, however, that the measure recently enacted by this parliament
February 12, 1979

to assist the lower middle income families in the form of a refundable child tax credit is far superior, both conceptually and practically, to the specific means of support suggested in the motion before us.
The hon. member would have the government consider a way of ensuring a global income corresponding to a family's needs. This is precisely the process that has been under way for several years and which led to the refundable child tax credit.
It surprises me that the hon. member would bring before this House a motion that is word for word the same as one he introduced previously and which was discussed in the House on two occasions last year, in one case by myself. The motion before us reflects none of the useful and constructive comments that were made by members of all parties in previous discussions. Most of all, it ignores the significant change which the new child tax credit represents in the way the federal government gives financial support to families with children.
In his motion and his remarks, the hon. member appears to recognize that many women have entered the labour force so that they and their families will be able to enjoy a decent standard of living. I wonder if he has considered how much money it would take to replace the lost earnings if these women were to stay at home as the hon. member would like them to. The figure would be in the billions of dollars. Where would the hon. member suggest we get this money? In December of last year, married women made up almost one quarter of the Canadian work force. Can the hon. member imagine the disastrous effect on the economy of this country if the contribution of these millions of women was lost?
Quite aside from any financial need to work outside the home, this government believes strongly that women as well as men, regardless of their marital or family situation, have an undeniable right to seek remunerative employment outside the home if they so choose. Suggestions such as the one implicit in this motion, that "a woman's place is in the home", particularly if reinforced financially as the hon. member suggests, lead to the creation of an atmosphere in which this basic right to a job can be questioned or denied. This is deplorable.
The motion would have us pay allowances to all "housewives who remain at home to look after their families." They are not even to be restricted to those with young children or to families in financial need. Clearly this is a measure aimed at keeping married women out of the work force. It is not clear why, in the absence of children, the performance of housework should by itself merit financial support from the government.
The hon. member has not yet given us any indication of how this allowance would be financed. Perhaps he would do this by taking away the family allowance and the child tax credit. He would be able to give those who stayed at home a bit more than they are getting now unless all the eligible women stayed home. Whatever increase he could finance in this way would not be large. It would not be large enough to persuade women from low income families to give up their jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just say, in the interest of saving time, that the first speaker suggested these things. I am asking questions, such as where would the money come from, and so on. But I would like to carry on.
As I said, many of these women will not give up their jobs, and their families would not have enough to live on. How would the hon. member explain to these women that he had taken away their baby bonuses and their tax credits to give the money to those who stayed home, if in fact that is what happened?
When the same motion was discussed in the House on February 27 of last year, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) expressed a view which I believe is shared by most Canadians. She said, as reported at page 3265 of Hansard:
If there is work to be done in the home it should be paid for by whoever is earning the living, be it the man or the woman.
There must never again be a Murdock case in Canada.
"Women and Pensions", a report produced last year by Kevin Collins for the Canadian Council on Social Development, adopted a similar view, concluding that the recognition of the value of housework should be enhanced through fundamental reform of the family law as it affects property. The report pointed out that current financial obligations between spouses are largely based on concepts on dependence and survival needs, rather than on a recognition of the value of housework or other unpaid contributions to the building up of family assets.
The principle of joint contribution to the acquisition of assets regardless of who pays the money out has not been widely established. This is, of course, an area which falls within provincial jurisdiction.

February 12, 1979
Housewives' Allowance
Pay for housework, the report also points out, does nothing to solve sexual division of labour inside and outside the home; it may simply serve to make it more rigid and to legitimize it. I would not want to see government interfere in family decisions in the way this motion suggests. To paraphrase an earlier statement of some renown, the state has no place in the kitchens of the nation.
I believe that the hon. member for Halton, that is me, Mr. Speaker, raised a very valid point in relation to this motion when it was last discussed in the Flouse. It is a point which well bears repeating. Rather than trying to keep women in the home, he suggested the need for much greater variety in the organization of our work life. In particular, a greater use of regularized part-time employment could benefit parents and enable them to utilize their skills and contribute to the family income while sharing in housework responsibilities. In this way, one parent, usually the woman, would not be forced into the lonely, isolated existence which too often characterizes the lot of the housewife.
As I pointed out, many mental health experts recommend part-time work for young mothers to help them overcome the sense of deprivation of not using their education and prior training, and to cope with the lack of contact and stimulation which they experience when they become new mothers. If society and employers were to recognize the legitimate place of regular part-time work in the work world, this isolation could be reduced and, along with it, problems such as alcoholism, and emotional disturbances which are too frequently experienced by housewives. Greater availability of part-time work on a continuing basis would also allow more fathers to share more equitably in the performance of household tasks.
The motion presented by the hon. member for Bellechasse refers to an allowance for housewives which would provide "an additional family income to that earned by the father." The proposal neglects the plight of single parent families which are predominantly headed by women. I might add, however, that an increasing proportion of these families are being headed by men. As with most existing welfare systems, the proposal would evidently exclude such men from assistance. Even in the case of sole-support mothers, the proposed measure would be inadequate. Even though the member for Bellechasse has acknowledged in his motion and earlier statements that two incomes are often necessary these days to meet the expenses of a family, he would say to sole-support working mothers, "Sorry, if you want help from us, you will have to quit your job and stay home."
In contrast with this attitude, the child tax credit which has been enacted by parliament will result in about $106 million in payments to single parent families this year. These sole-support parents, of whom over 90 per cent are women, will not have to stay at home in order to receive this assistance. Of the money going to this group, $35 million will be a net gain to the lowest income single parent families, who are almost all headed by women.

In total, $810 million will be paid to women in the form of the refundable tax credit entirely to those in middle and lower income families. Despite the reduction in family allowance payments, women, as a group, will be getting $120 million more this year in payments than they would have under the previous system. The measure proposed by this motion is intended "to ensure a global income corresponding to the family's needs."
Successive governments in this country have recognized for over thirty years that there is a need for intervention in the way in which the free market system distributes its rewards. As impressive as it is as a generator of wealth and income, the market system, if left to itself, does not ensure that all of our citizens will receive income adequate to their needs and those of their families. Wage rates are set without regard to the financial needs of their recipients. This is as it must be if the system is to operate efficiently. Clearly there is a role for the government in compensating for this market failure.
The Marsh report on social security in Canada recognized this over thirty years ago when it recommended the introduction of family allowances. The then prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, stated that society had a responsibility to assist in the costs of child rearing.
Child benefits delivered by means of the income tax system have an even longer history in Canada than family allowances. Child tax exemptions were introduced in 1918 only one year after the start of the income tax system itself. It is interesting to note that for a brief period during the Second World War the exemptions were replaced by non-refundable child tax credits.
Family allowances were introduced in 1945 to complement the tax benefits. The federal child benefits system grew in importance to the extent that, last year, it distributed about $2.7 billion to Canadian families, with most of this being paid directly to mothers.
It was recognized, however, that despite this assistance, there were still nearly 600,000 families with over 1 million children living in poverty. Studies of the children from such families have shown that they are more likely to be sick than children from other families. They are also more likely to be severely retarded in their physical development. As a result of these difficulties, children from poorer families are less likely to perform well in school and hence are too likely to end up in low paying dead-end jobs. They, in turn, are unable to provide adequately for the needs of their children, and the cycle begins again.
The social and economic costs of this tragedy are enormous. Pressures on government-provided social and health services are increased. The connection between poverty and crime and violence is also well recognized, particularly in our urban areas. We are all losers when thousands of our fellow Canadians live in poverty.
It was with these considerations in mind that the recent changes to our child benefits system were enacted. The effort was made to get more assistance to those families which most
February 12, 1979

needed it. The government was looking for ways to reduce the level of government spending, and yet at the same time it recognized the need to help low and middle income families. The introduction of the refundable child tax credit combined with other changes was seen as a way of achieving greater fairness and doing a better job with the resources at our disposal.
As hon. members are aware, the child tax credit is refundable. This important feature will mean that benefits will be received by families whose incomes are too low to be taxable, as well as by those in the middle income ranges. Two thirds of Canadian families will receive benefits from this new measure.
There are admittedly some additional administrative costs associated with this new approach. Compared to alternative ways of concentrating the benefits at the low and middle ranges of the income scale, however, the approach adopted is a sensible one. Furthermore, the benefits to be derived more than justify the additional costs.
For recipients of the child tax credit who have not previously been required to fill out tax returns, there may be some initial confusion. The measures announced by the Minister of National Flealth and Welfare (Miss Begin) to assist people in applying for these benefits should go a long way toward overcoming this problem. Ways of simplifying the procedure are being examined for application in future.
It is interesting that the motion before us speaks of the global family income, because this is precisely the concept that is being used to determine the amount of benefit each family will get from this measure. This approach was adopted because the government wanted to make the benefit correspond more closely to a family's need for assistance than would have been the case with a universal payment or if only the income of one parent had been considered.
Despite the reduction in the level of family allowances, this program will remain the largest single federal child-related program and will continue to be the foundation of the federal system of benefits. It will also remain fully indexed to the cost of living, as will the new child tax credit.
The new system that we have adopted is significantly fairer than the one in place previously. Low income families will now receive greater federal benefits than will high income families. This was not the case in the past and was the object of justifiable criticism from several quarters, including the National Council of Welfare in their report called "The Hidden Welfare System".

Mr. Speaker, I think we are indebted once again to the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for bringing this particular motion before us. In the previous debate which took place in this House a little less than a year ago the matter received support from all sides of the House, with a number of very definite reservations. I do not think that, in the main, these reservations have changed very much.
I am most intrigued by the government's response this year as compared to last year, at least if that is the one that can be
Housewives' Allowance
measured by the remarks of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook). I think that hon. member has, at least in some ways, improved the response from the government side in respect of this measure. He needs a bit more practise, perhaps, in reading, as indicated by the fact that when he started to quote himself he began by saying "he". I think, more seriously, he should do a bit more research in the area of child tax credit, particularly when he asserts, as he did almost as the main part of his speech, that the child tax credit meets a particular situation in recognizing the economic and social benefits of women in the home. I think that we need to do more research in terms of its impact with respect to women.
I was interested to note that the major concern of the hon. member for Halton was that the motion would have an impact on taking women out of employment situations outside the home, that it would create pressure to take women out of the market place and the mainstream of the economy, thereby forcing them back into a home-making situation. If the hon. member thinks that that is a problem, I suggest that he look at the principle which was adopted in the child tax credit bill. I will not repeat it because it was dealt with at some length both by myself and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald).
There are problems which are created by the principle which the hon. member referred to, in terms of the global family income assessment. From the standpoint of making a determination of greatest need, one can find little fault with the approach. But it is not a matter of dealing with the husband and wife in a position of equal equity at this point, because it is well established that the average income of women in our society for the same kind of employment that a man might do is only 60 per cent of that earned by the male counterpart. This is an indication that we still have a long way to go with respect to any kind of income equality.
The implication which is very much a part of the child tax credit plan is that there will be subtle and, perhaps, not so subtle pressures created to take women out of the work force and to force them, against their will, back into a domestic situation. I think it would have been useful if the hon. member for Halton had raised as well the problems in connection with the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. We are still hearing the repercussions of that exercise.
If the hon. member had read the briefs by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and the National Advisory Council on the Status of Women he would have found a number of reasons why they object to the approach which is being taken and which was creating a number of problems for women in the work force. However, that is not the substance of the motion before us this afternoon.
Since the hon. member for Bellechasse presented his motion, there has been more up to date information which has attempted to put a value on the work created in the home. In a study done in May, 1978, by Queen's University, they came up with a value of $60 billion, or one third of the gross national

February 12, 1979
Housewives' Allowance
product on work created in the home. A report by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women which came out in June, 1978, entitled, "Five Million Women, a Study of the Canadian Housewife", concurred with the finding, that the figure for work done in the home was very substantial.
The important aspect of the motion before us today, and which was before us last February 27, as I see it, is the recognition by society of the importance of the work done in the home. Quite obviously, this is the problem with which society and, up until now, the major organs of society, such as this House of Commons, have not adequately wrestled. As I said almost a year ago, I agree that more adequate economic and social recognition must be given to women who remain at home, indeed, not just to women, but men or women who remain at home.
I went on at some length in previous remarks on this same motion about the way in which lifestyles are changing to the point that increasingly men as well as women are taking on the domestic responsibilities in the home when they move out of the work force. Ideally, at some future point this is the kind of equilibrium we would like to achieve.
The hon. member for Halton quoted from a section of the Canadian Council on Social Development report having to do with women's pensions. His quotation bears repeating because it is the nub of the problem which we presently face, and that is that the pay-for-housework proposal does nothing to solve the sexual division of labour inside and outside the home. So far in this debate, this problem has not been referred to, but there is an acute and present problem having to do with elderly women in poverty as consequence of the many earning years they have spent at home raising families, looking after spouses and, as a result, not being eligible to contribute to pension plans.
According to recent statistics, the percentage of unattached women living in poverty jumped from 41.2 per cent to 45 per cent as of November, 1978. The percentage of unattached elderly over 70 living in poverty jumped from 58.1 per cent to 63.2 per cent, most of these people being women. Obviously there is a very pressing need to initiate some action with respect to the desperate straits in which older single women find themselves in our society, whether they are women who have worked for the greater part of their lives as single women, or women who have cared for families and who have been left in a destitute state in their later years.
In the advisory council report which was produced in June, they came up with a figure of some five million Canadian women who are performing up to 60 hours of work in the home per week. It should be recognized at the outset that the people who work in the home are not in a normal employment situation where they have an opportunity to report for work at a specific time, coffee breaks at mid-morning and mid-afternoon, or time off for lunch, personal duties, responsibilities, and so on. When we talk of women in the home, we are talking about women who work longer hours than in any other form of employment in our society, people who must work sometimes under extreme pressure, particularly during those years of

heavy responsibility while raising a young family. Yet in no way have we tried to look at the responsibility of society with regard to people in the home.
The June report of the advisory council said that housewives should be compensated for their contributions and that economic ways should be found, including such things as guaranteed annual incomes, special provisions within the Canada Pension Plan or inclusion of housewives in general social insurance plans.
We are far removed from reaching that achievement. The closest we have come was in the discussions we had in this House last year with respect to the problems of taxation affecting farmers who, in many instances, employ their wives, or small businessmen who employ their wives and they are not allowed to make the proper income tax deductions which recognize the real contribution that spouses make in those forms of industry and activity regarded as small business. There has been a real failure by governments to examine their responsibilities with respect to the largest form of employment that exists, and that is the home. As the advisory council stated in June, "pension policies should take into account that pensions are assets and therefore should be included in the splitting of the marital assets based on the equal contribution of each spouse." The contribution would come from work performed both outside and inside the home. In other words, the advisory council on the status of women suggested that the time has come to place an economic value on housework to give it the basis which it deserves.
It is interesting to note that so far in the efforts to achieve recognition of the importance of housework to society, even the most minimal kinds of recognition have been ignored. Some members will recall that just a few weeks ago the National Council of Women was here to meet with the cabinet and respresentatives of all parties. One of their major requests which they have put forward on previous occasions was that homemaking be included as a recognized occupation under the occupational index of the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we can go that far. I am sorry that so far this has not been referred to by the government side, but I would think that this is one matter on which all members can agree-a beginning of recognition of the importance of homemaking to the economy so that it could be included as one of the recognized occupations in the occupational index.
There is very basically an issue here which I think the hon. member for Bellechasse has quite rightly brought to our attention with repeated emphasis, and that is that women in the home make a contribution that in no way has been recognized, either in terms of any kind of allowance or compensation or tax recognition, or even in terms of the recognized pension programs that deal with the plight of elderly women in our society.
I think, Mr. Speaker, we must also recognize that if we were to enact this particular provision by itself, without recognizing
February 12, 1979

the particular problems that women are presently encountering in maintaining their right to be a part of the over-all work force of our society, we might at this period cause a very serious dislocation.
As members will know, I and other members in this House have been troubled by the increasing references by members of the government to the problems that are created by the economy when women are increasing their participation in the work force. I think this does no credit whatsoever to the over-all economic strategy of the government in terms of trying to achieve greater employment opportunity for both men and women. I think that again this motion by itself would add only further momentum to the kind of misunderstanding and misdirection created by the government with respect to its attitude to women in the work force. However, Mr. Speaker, I think the essential principle-and that is the recognition of the contribution, both economically and socially made by people in the home, whether it be women or men-is rightfully brought to our attention. I would hope that in a further debate on this matter not only will we hear from the member for Halton, who is very interested in the issue, but also from the minister who has the responsibility for the status of women.
