speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying this afternoon, not only did the actuarial commission find out that the government had confused the true cost of the plan with the amounts it was setting aside, but the actuarial commission reported that the assumptions in the government's valuation were not realistic. In particular, they pointed to one specific pair of assumptions. First, even though pensions will be paid based upon final salary, no salary increases will occur, and second that although the fund was earning 7.6 per cent, it would only earn 4 per cent interest. In other words, the chief actuary was implicitly assuming that some of his assumptions offset each other. He was explicitly underestimating the cost of the plan by assuming that no future salary increases would take place, and hoping that this would be balanced out by explicitly underestimating the amount of interest earned by the fund.
I am sure individually these assumptions do not make sense. They do not reflect reality. It is even questionable whether taken together they make sense. But I would like to stress that at no time did the chief actuary ever indicate that the only interest required to be earned by the fund to provide the benefits was 4 per cent. He merely used this low interest rate, together with no provision for future salary increases, to simplify the calculation.
The consultants found that on the basis of their best estimates the combined cost of the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act for current employees was 15.3 per cent of payroll, and the current year's cost for past service benefits amounted to an additional 19.1 per cent of payroll. This 34 per cent compares with an average employer current service cost in the private sector of 5 to 6 per cent of payroll.
The consultants also found that no conclusion could be drawn as to whether the total compensation of the public sector was greater than the total compensation of the private sector, for a rather interesting reason. In spite of the fact that total compensation comparability was explicit government policy, and we still have a bill before this House saying it is explicit government policy, the government had never made a study to find out what the facts were. According to the actuarial report, the impression created by the basic facts paper that the value of pensions for federal public servants was no better than that found in the private sector was false.
The consultants made several specific recommendations; several of these affect this bill directly. They recommended that a valuation of the combined plan be made with each plan change. They recommended that these valuation assumptions be made as realistic as possible. They recommended that a valuation of the combined plan occur at least every three years. They recommended that the contributions to the plan

February 12, 1979

should be made in line with the results of the valuation as is required in the private sector.
In response to the actuarial report, the then president of the treasury board indicated that he was going to make changes which were "just and fair in terms of their impact on taxpayers", however at the same time "the principle of maintaining the purchasing value of pensions ... is a principle to which the government is committed and remains committed." It is rather interesting how he married these conclusions. He started by stating that there are experts who feel that we can count on seeing a long-term situation in which interest rates will be 3 per cent to 4 per cent ahead of the rate of inflation.
1 find that interesting because the only five-year period over the past 55 years in which the real return was 4 per cent or above was the first five years of the great depression. I will admit that there are many experts who believe that this government's economic policies are leading us inexorably into the next depression, but surely that is not something the government wants to count on in setting up its pension plans.
On the other hand, it is possible that those experts reside in the Department of Finance. In fact, it may be that one of the so-called experts is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). After all, he has been feeding out highly optimistic Financial estimates to this House since he took over the portfolio.
The fact is, there are experts and there are experts. Some, like the finance minister, have no credibility. Others are well respected. I believe we have a duty to find out just what well-known economists are predicting real returns at this level. In fact the only period that we have seen of real returns of over 3 per cent are years in which we had changes in the consumer price index of less than 4 per cent. This 4 per cent was the original objective under the anti-inflation program, but then that was just another of this government's over-optimistic forecasts.
In any case, having introduced these experts, the President of the Treasury Board indicated that he saw two basic choices; one was to continue the current plan and see which of these so-called experts were correct; the other was to introduce immediately a set of ad hoc adjustments. The minister of that time said that in his view the stakes, namely, the welfare of future taxpayers and pensioners, are just too high to gamble on continuing the current arrangements.
When the government introduced the new arrangements it was gambling as well, gambling with the lives of our public servants. Yet the implication in what was said is that somehow it has reduced the risk.
What we have before us now is something even more nebulous than what we were presented with in 1973. In 1973, we at least knew half of the equation, we knew what level of benefits our pensioners were likely to get. We did not know what it would cost.
With this legislation we do not have the cost estimates once again. But this time we do not have any idea what level of
Pensions
benefits will be provided in the future. The government is asking us to buy a pig in a poke, to pay an unknown price for a series of unknown benefits. We owe our public more than this. We have to find out what the price of these benefits is for the general public, and similarly we ought to ensure public servants that they will receive a decent pension, a pension reasonably related to future changes in the cost of living.
That is the purpose of the two questions that 1 asked in the House on November 3. I am concerned that these ad hoc arrangements will not deliver adequate benefits to our retired public servants. I am particularly concerned because of the way the plan is divided into the three groups consisting of the RCMP, the armed forces and the public service. Before we adopt any plan which changes this multi-billion dollar plan, we owe it to ourselves and to our public to ensure that in the future the plan produces reasonable benefits at a reasonable cost.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) earlier today spoke of his willingness to accept slight reductions in benefits at this time. We know that over the first three years the public servants would not be entitled to full indexing. However, we have no idea from this government what level of indexing will be provided for in the future. Will it be one half the cost of living or one quarter? Just what is the government proposing? What are the public servants likely to receive under inflationary conditions in the future? That is a question that must be answered before we vote on this bill.
The second part of my question of November 3 had to do directly with the cost of the program. As I indicated, it appears to me, and certainly I am willing to be corrected by the President of the Treasury Board, that the changes which have been introduced will place a greater burden on the public treasury to support the public service superannuation account, a burden which could be in the order of a hundred million dollars each and every year.
This transfer arises because of the use made of that arbitrary 4 per cent interest assumption. I mentioned earlier the fact that the chief actuary assumed a yield of 4 per cent on the money to offset the assumption that there were going to be no future salary increases. This did not mean at all that he only needed 4 per cent interest. He needed the excess interest earnings to offset the deficiency in the salary assumption. Yet what the government is proposing to do, Mr. Speaker, is to give these so-called excess earnings from retired pensioners' accounts to support their indexed pensions.
We heard the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) taking just one side of the equation today. He talked about the excess interest earnings, the windfall gains in interest that are made. If there are high interest rates in the future, it will likely be because inflation is out of control again. If there are high interest rates, there are high rates of salary increases. If there are windfall gains in interest, there are windfall losses because of the salary increases, because we guaranteed to pay a pension based upon the final salary. That is a very simple idea. One offsets the other. He cannot do what the government has just done and take the excess earnings on the interest, say that

February 12, 1979
Pensions
is for the pensioners, and the excess losses, because of future inflation, are for the taxpayer, yet that is what this government is trying to do in this bill.
We had serious questions raised in this House about the cost of the total plan, and particularly the cost of indexing. What the government appears to have done is primarily to transfer an unknown amount of money over from the Public Service Superannuation Act to support the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act and somehow pretend that everything is all right if the matching contributions plus these additional transfers make the indexing portion work. I think this is just a sham; it is a flim-flam. You cannot just transfer money from one side to another and say, "Look, the other side is now fine." That is Dagwood and Blondie economics. It reminds me of a situation where Dagwood and Blondie each have $30 and they both need to buy a $40 item. Blondie says to Dagwood, "Give me $10, then I will have $40 and at least one of us will be better off." In other words, forget what is happening on the other side. There is no more money created by this little exercise.
We have to look at both plans in combination and find out what is the additional public liability as a result of transferring these earnings out of the PSSA. Certainly it appears to me that what it will do is to increase the experience deficiencies of the PSSA dramatically.
In any case we do not know if it is still proposed to credit the pensioners with the excess over 4 per cent, since it is my understanding that the valuation which is being prepared will be made using realistic assumptions and the 4 per cent may not itself appear in the valuation any longer. We do not know, because the report due December, 1977, has still not appeared in spite of our requests that it be produced. Besides these two specific items, what the benefits will cost and what the benefits would look like, I have other reservations with the bill.
The bill should contain a provision to value the plan every three years, or prior to any subsequent plan amendment. This valuation should also include benefit projections.
In addition, question No. 556 that I placed on the order paper on November 9 was designed to give us essential information to judge this bill. How can we comment on the bill with no financial data presented by the government? In particular, I feel it is necessary to look at a projection on the amount of future indexing available for each of the three categories of employees separately, the armed forces, the RCMP and the civil service. I believe that what the government is doing in this bill is intrinsically weakening the funding basis for retired pensioners. It may well be that the ad hoc arrangements of their indexing come unhinged for one group before the others. If there is one group going to come unhinged, it will be the veterans. The House must find out when the indexing is going to break down.
Another question was designed to raise the point about the rate of interest credited to the fund. This has been a point of contention with public servants for some time. They feel they have not been credited with the rate of interest they could get

if investments in private securities were allowed. Of course it is not necessary actually to invest in outside securities at all to credit a higher rate of interest. The current plan, after all, doesn't invest in real securities either; a hypothetical fund is set up to determine the amount of interest payable. The hypothetical fund could just as soon assume some other type of investment.
However, many Canadian actuaries have expressed great concern about our country's ability to pay for these phantom-funded plans because of the significant demographic changes which are going to occur in Canada over the next 50 years as the baby boom passes through into retirement. This is a point the hon. member for Ottawa West raised today. What is the difference? The difference is that with the phantom-funded plans we have now there are no real assets. The only asset we have is the future taxing power of the government.
With the demographic changes which will take place in this country, with the rapid increase in retirees as compared with the working population, I think we should give very serious consideration to the-

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa West on a point of order.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member if he considers the public debt of Canada to be absolutely insignificant and worthless. Is not the asset of a Public Service Superannuation Fund just as real, just as valid, just as good as any security of the Government of Canada?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
That is exactly what I have said. The point is that the rate at which we are building up debt is a source of concern to me because future taxpayers will be called upon to make good those obligations. And we owe it to the people of Canada to investigate just what that tax load is going to be in the future to pay off these obligations when they come due. For these reasons I ask whether any consideration is being given to setting aside some portion of the liability in real assets, not just hypothetical funds.
Again, the hon. member for Ottawa West said we had no choice, that we couldn't interfere in the private sector. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that if the hon. member takes the time to investigate he will find out that a reasonable portion-a small but growing one-of the Quebec pension plan is invested in the private sector. It is doing so without unduly influencing the private market. I am not suggesting that the whole fund should be invested in the private sector. Not at all! That would be quite another matter. But I think there is some merit to building up some portion of the fund in real assets.
I would like to make one final point in relation to this bill, Mr. Speaker. In Bill C-56, the amendments to the Income Tax Act, brought before the House last spring, the Minister of Finance restricted the rights of an individual citizen to retire before age 60 if they were funding their retirement plan with an RRSP. I talked today about the public perception that public servants have been set aside as a special breed in society. Here is another direct example. Public servants are
February 12, 1979

allowed to retire on full pension at age 55. Individuals outside the public service are prohibited from having access to their retirement funds-their RRSP fund-for pension purposes until age 60. Not only that, the public servant receives a thousand dollar annual tax exempt income from age 55, while the RRSP policy holder, even if he takes money from age 60, does not get his tax exemption until age 65.
I am not for the moment suggesting that public servants should be restricted from retiring at age 60. However, I do believe the two acts should be brought into harmony. We cannot continue to have one rule for the public servants and another rule-designed by public servants-which is more restrictive for the rest of the public. We would be perpetuating an unfair discrimination between the retiring age at which members of the general public can have access to their pensions in the form of RRSPs and the age at which public servants can have their pensions. This House should consider directly harmonizing RRSP provisions with the early retirement provisions granted public servants.
This is a period of wide-scale cynicism and skepticism on the part of the public with respect to the government. What we have before us today is another bill to change the public service pensions, a bill for which so far we have no cost-estimates for the changes contemplated. On the contrary, we have what might be construed as a deliberate concealing of the cost effects of the PSSA. We have been provided with no benefit projections so that that public service might have some idea what they are paying for. The sort of cynicism 1 mentioned will only be magnified if the government continues to lay important financial bills in front of this House without providing any financial data.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, what I have been saying is that we face two obligations when considering any bill of the sort before us. We have an obligation to the general public, and we have an obligation to the public servants. In order to fulfil these twin obligations we must have some figures presented to us upon which to make an intelligent decision. In addition, we should ensure that from this point on such figures are provided us regularly, every three years, or upon any planned amendment, to ensure that parliament retains financial control over substantial expenditures. In the absence of any financial information how can we approve this bill? How can we commit the public of Canada and the public servants of Canada to this plan when we have no idea of what the plan actually is?
No wonder our economy under this government is in such dire straits today. Today we know that in 1973 we spent $6 billion. But we found that out only last year. Almost without thought we committed ourselves to spend that money. Today we are being asked to make future plans in the dark once again. Why? The real problem underlying this bill lies with inflation, not indexing. What we need to do is direct our attention to bringing down inflation. The hon. member for Ottawa West said today we have to learn to live with inflation. That is not something the party to which I belong accepts at all. That is Liberal philosophy. We have to take control of our
Pensions
financial expenditures in this country, and this bill is a good place with which to start.
I believe we must support this bill on second reading, if only to get it into committee. Then in committee the government will, hopefully, present us with some information on which to base our consideration of the bill. I cannot believe the government would present such a bill to parliament without evaluation, without benefit projections. Surely we have a right to see them. The public must be served. If we do not have the right to see them, if the government denies us this essential information, surely the public will condemn this government once more for its economic flim-flammery.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak extremely briefly on Bill C-12. I intend to do so because I support the bill strongly. I support the comments made on Thursday evening by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan), the speech by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and the excellent speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis).
My reason for rising to enter this debate is the fact that early on when this became a public issue and the National Citizens Coalition started their campaign, I replied that I disagreed with their approach and that in my view it was full of error. I put together and distributed a statement, and some of the organizations within the public service which came across the statement thought it had a good deal of merit. They, in turn, circulated it across the country because it was supportive of adequate public service pensions and, indeed, of adequate pensions in general. I suppose it was because of this that the National Citizens' Coalition decided they should apply a lot of pressure to myself and they did so through a variety of means.
Therefore, I thought I should stand in my place this evening and put on record the essential points which were made in the statement I read some time ago in response to their original misrepresentation. I regret the National Citizens' Coalition did what they did. It developed a good deal of ill will toward public servants which they in no way deserve. In my opinion Canada is well served by its public servants, and the kind of insinuations made about them were very disagreeable for the public servants to bear.
At a meeting after this became a public issue I asked some people what they thought the average pension of a public servant really was. Some of the responses were $15,000, $16,000 or $20,000 a year. I think I am fairly accurate in saying that the average number of years a public servant works is 25 and that after that length of service his retirement pension is about $5,100 a year. When people understand that, they begin to think that the issue raised by the National Citizens' Coalition is pretty phony.
I think the National Citizen's Coalition is running a stalking horse in its intervention so that people in the private sector

February 12, 1979
Pensions
who resist setting up an adequate pension plan for employees in the private sector will not have to begin thinking in terms of putting together a pension plan which would provide adequate benefits for employees.
So far in this debate spokesmen for all parties-at least the principal spokesmen-essentially agree with the provisions of the bill. More importantly, they have joined in opposing the National Citizens' Coalition. However, 1 am not sure 1 can say that in all sincerity about the previous speaker, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan).
The hon. member for York-Scarborough represents the opinion which is expressed very often by supporters of his party. I hope hon. members opposite follow the lead of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and attempt to convince their supporters that his is the stance they should be taking. I am sure there are many supporters of the official opposition who will be amazed that the hon. member for Hamilton West should take such a moderate stand. I think he has taken a rather progressive point of view on this bill.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext: That is what I am, a Progressive Conservative.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton West for doing that, but I am sure his stand is not in tune with some of the things which are being said by some of the supporters of his party who try to pursue the argument that somehow the public service has a very rich pension plan, that the private sector could in no way afford such a plan, and that somehow that would amount to a tremendous liability for the taxpayer.
There are really two basic questions at stake here. One is support for good pension plans, both private and public. The hon. member for York-Scarborough seemed to be putting forward the argument put forward vigorously by the National Citizens' Coalition, that we should be pulling down public service pensions rather than that in the private sector there is a need to increase pensions so that people working in that sector have adequate protection. It seems to me that many of those who associate themselves with that school of thought have never worked on farms or known the rural communities in that part of Canada where I was born and grew up years ago. People who were not owners of farms and who worked out as hired men did not enjoy favourable retirement conditions because they were very poorly paid during their working years. It was very difficult for them to put money aside for retirement. Anyone from that kind of environment has to be a strong supporter of adequate pensions.
I am delighted that the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre argued that point. They did so very well. The issue is adequate pensions for all Canadians, not tearing down the public service pension system which has been established.
The President of the Treasury Board established in his speech that the basic pension plan is very sound actuarially and that Bill C-12 would make the indexing provision of the plan actuarially sound. In the statement I prepared, a condi-

tion upon which I said I would support public service pensions is that there must be an adequate pension, but it must be actuarially sound. There must be a decrease in the pay-out to accomplish that, and Bill C-12 does that. That was the part of the argument of the previous speaker which I did not follow. He said that somehow there was no information available as to what this would cost if parliament should commit itself by passing this bill.
I think the President of the Treasury Board was very clear when he said in his speech that the question now would be how much pension could be paid with the money available, not how much it would cost, and I invite the hon. member for York-Scarborough to read the comments of the President of the Treasury Board because the answer to the very questions the hon. member was raising is the basis of the bill.
Another point I made in my statement is that, for the life of me, I cannot follow the line of argument which essentially says that we should not have good pensions. In the absence of good pensions the needs of people in their retirement years will have to be funded from the tax base. I am amazed that the National Citizens' Coalition should not support the argument that it is better to have employees contribute to an adequate pension plan for their retirement years during their employment years. If we argue against pension plans, then we must also argue that after retirement, when there is great need, the government will have to help in a substantial way.
I am sure we all remember that a few years ago the pensions of teachers, nurses and other groups were very modest and not indexed. After a period of inflation those pensions became very inadequate. There were strong representations to governments about how inadequate those pensions were, and after a time governments were obligated to put very large lump sum payments into those plans in order to improve them so that people on those pensions could go on. That is not a good way to go about supporting Canadians in their retirement years. However, that seems to be exactly the argument the National Citizens' Coalition has been making.
The major provisions in this bill regarding indexing not beginning until age 60 are fair. The proportioning of the amount of indexing available to a person at retirement, given the date of retirement, is very fair. We all know about the advantages enjoyed previously by those retiring in the last days of December. On January 1 of the following year they had the advantage of a full year of indexing. I think that is very unfair to those paying into the plan. I think it is taking advantage of the plan, and changing that should surely be accepted by the public service and supported by all hon. members.
The basic theory of the bill regarding the amount of pension the plan can afford is also good. I am pleased that the President of the Treasury Board feels that there should be a basic amount available so that people who earned low salaries and wages throughout their working lives can have at least a base upon which to operate rather than a completely comparative type of pension plan.
One question raised by the hon. member for Hamilton West the other night was the question of why there has not been an
February 12, 1979

opportunity for the public service to increase their contributions, given the fact that as an employee group they do contribute, on a percentage basis, as high a percentage as any employee group of which I am aware. That is a good point, but I think even the public service recognizes that the indexing provision of the plan at the present time cannot be actuarially sound and therefore there are two options, one to gear down the pay-out so that it balances, and another to contribute voluntarily over a year or so a higher percentage of salary so that there can be full indexing without any liability to the taxpayer. There may very well be good reasons why both those options were not offered, and I think when this bill is in committee this might be explored to see whether there is in fact a possibility in that regard.
I represent a very large number of air traffic controllers in my riding by virtue of the fact that Toronto International Airport is located on the boundary of my riding. I think the special provision in the bill for air traffic controllers is fair and just. It is a provision for which they have argued over the years, and I was glad to see that provision in Bill C-12 in terms of their indexing procedure.
I just wanted to make the point that for quite some time I have been upset by the approach of the National Citizens' Coalition and the kind of half truths which they have put forward. This has done a great deal of damage to the credibility of the public service. I want it to be put on the record that 1 support the provision of adequate pensions for all Canadians. The issue should be whether or not all Canadians have adequate pensions, rather than the argument that because public servants have contributed more than any other group on a percentage basis they should have a good pension. I wonder why the National Citizens' Coalition, and some of the people in the business community who support their argument as strongly as they do, do not see the value of my argument. It is far better to have an employee contribute to an adequate pension plan during his or her working years than to give him a small pension and have him look to the government to supplement it from the tax basis during his retirement years.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity I had to contribute to the debate briefly.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to confine my remarks tonight to the RCMP and the manner in which this bill affects that force. I will be somewhat critical of certain aspects of it in so far as it concerns the force. I happened to hear the hon. member who has just resumed his seat refer to air traffic controllers. The bill contains a provision to establish a special pension program, which was agreed to by the government in 1976, I believe, for air traffic controllers in operational or tower service. In effect, the provisions bring them increased pension benefits, in addition to the 2 per cent of salary which is contributed by controllers once the bill takes effect and is matched by the employer in order to pay for these benefits.
Pensions
There is a good reason behind those special provisions. Air traffic controllers in operational or tower duties operate, particularly at heavy density traffic aerodromes such as Toronto, Montreal and others, under very heavy stress. They have in their hands the lives of crews and passengers of literally hundreds of aircraft coming in and out of those airports daily. So there should be special provisions for them. They burn out.
A somewhat similar argument can be made with respect to those who serve in maximum security penitentiaries in the country, and indeed that is one of their annually recurring submissions with respect to their retirement plans. The stress factor applies even more forcefully to members of the police forces, not just the RCMP but any police force, particularly those in the larger metropolitan centres. I will quote briefly now from the Canadian Police Chief issue of January, 1979, from an article by inspector Charles Massey, police chaplain with the Ontario Provincial Police. The article begins as follows:
The evening news has just ended. It's 11.30 p.m. She went in to check the kids and re-tuck them in. She returned to the living room, sat sleeping in front of the late movie and waited for Jack to return from the 4-12 shift. It was a good movie and she didn't notice the time passing. Later, glancing at her watch, she saw 1.30. "Where's Jack?... must have had a late call", she thought. Fifteen minutes later she heard a car pull into the driveway and its door close. Then the doorbell rang. " ... must have forgotten his key." She opened the door and there stood the Detachment Commander and the Chaplain. "Mary, there's been an accident. .. Jack's been shot... he's dead . . ."
That is not an isolated sort of occurrence. That has happened so far, during 1978 at any rate, some 50 to 60 times in Canada. Just last week a member of the force was killed in the Yukon. What happens? There is a separate pension fund for dependants of members of the force, but the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act, which has to be considered when considering this kind of legislation, is still in the dark ages so far as the treatment of dependants of officers of the force is concerned.
Consider this other example of an officer who was killed on duty who had over five years of service. Under the pension continuation act, the widow and children of that deceased member of the force are entitled to 50 per cent of his entitlement. If we refer to the pension superannuation act, we find that if a member of the force dies with less than ten years service, his widow and/or children receive a return of his contributions or an amount equal to one month's pay for each year of pensionable service, whichever is greater. Contribution of single members are payable to their estate. That certainly would not take a widow with three or four small children very far.
Let us consider another example, and I purposely avoid names here. This is an example of a member of the force in the maritimes who had served 21 years in the force and died of a heart attack. He left a wife and five children, the oldest was 16 and the youngest was two years of age. That widow and her five children are living on a pension of $490 a month. I believe-and I believe that that belief is shared by all members of the House-that that is a disgraceful way to treat members of a fine force such as the RCMP and their dependants in circumstances such as I have outlined. There is no way that a

February 12, 1979
Pensions
widow with five growing children can survive on $490 a month.
This is current data from which I will quote now. I am not going back to the days when my father received a grand total of $93 a month as his pension after 30 years of service. That sort of a situation cannot be allowed to continue, I suggest. Adequate provision must be made for the special nature of the force and for the dependants of the deceased members of the force who meet their end while serving or while on duty.
I want to say a word or two about the stress factor, but before that let me just quote one or two significant statistics from the force. During 1975 and 1976 there were 747 members who left the force of their own volition. They chose to do so prior to becoming eligible for a pension. Only 286 received a pension in the same period. In other words, it is more attractive to leave the force than to remain in until pensioned. There is no real incentive, pensionwise, for members to serve out their period in the force and go to pension.
The statistics are also significant for another reason. They show that the force cannot, I submit, be compared to other facets of the civil service, with the odd exception such as air traffic controllers in operational tower duty or, perhaps, prison guards. The force cannot be compared to other facets of the public service precisely because of the stress factor, shift work and the days off situation, particularly where families are concerned.
It is far too easy to say that a person knew the situation before he got the job, but complete understanding cannot be gained until one is completely immersed in the job. The police force job is not the same as an industrial job. A man in industry does not have to face the problem of having to stop a car in the middle of the night looking for a dangerous criminal, not knowing whether he will be met with a sawed-off shotgun. That man's wife is not wondering if he is coming home at shift end, two, three, four, 24 hours later, or never.
The stress factor is very well documented and I do not have the opportunity of going into it in any great detail now. The force, indeed, has commissioned a study which should be completed by now and should be made available to members as rapidly as possible in order that this kind of legislation will not appear before us again without some adequate remedies for the situations I have described.
At the present time in the force the pension of a member is based on the average salary over the last six years' service, but to state that at 35 years' service one is eligible to receive 70 per cent of salary as pension is very misleading. That, indeed, is not the fact. If one is to consider a sergeant retiring after 25 years' service with six years in the ranks, one is led to believe he is eligible to receive 50 per cent of his salary, when in fact he receives only 41 per cent of his salary at retirement. Similarly, at 35 years' service he in fact only receives 58 per cent of salary on the day of retirement.
The theory behind pensions, as I understand it, is that having given the best years of their lives to the service, their

country and their government, they are entitled to a minimum of security at retirement. They do not have that now, and certainly it is glaringly apparent that their widows and dependants do not have that now.
We have heard opinions about the effects of inflation here tonight. It is my view that inflation is caused by the government, and members of the force have absolutely no way of defending against it. The inducement of a pension when a member of the force was recruited was an influencing factor in many cases of those joining the force. Most members leave the force with 24 years' service, not because they want to but because they must in order to take advantage of their youth in gaining other employment to meet the needs of their families at a critical time in their lives. They are fully aware that the pension they are to receive will not sustain them in any dignity or standard of living.
Most police forces in the United States permit members to retire on 20 years' service with half salary. There are other advantages as well. I want to draw for members some very startling comparisons. For instance, in the state of Alaska state troopers operate under this plan. The contributions are 5 per cent of salary; contributions earn 4.5 per cent interest; pension benefits are available at any time after five years' service; normal retirement is at 20 years' service at half salary; salary is averaged over the past three years, and that is the way it used to be in the force and the way they want to return to now; thirty years is maximum service, or 55 years of age; pension cost of living is indexed at 4 per cent if the fund is solvent; benefits are tax exempt; there is a 10 per cent increase in benefits if the receiver is a resident of the state of Alaska, an inducement to stay there; benefits are stacked to social security; no-cost medical insurance to the receiver and dependants; when the plan is fully funded the administrator can make investments in the private sector, with funds realizing current interest rates; and there are three separate operational survivor plans for dependants.
Contrast that with the treatment we accord in our pension legislation to members of one of the finest, if not the finest, police forces in the world. Are the United States pension funds being bankrupted? I suggest that is not the case.
Police work is an occupation requiring the stamina of youth, and that is particularly so of the RCMP. Many recognized authorities on police administration and psychology take the position that the stress factor in the police profession is the symptom of higher rates of suicide, marriage breakdown, alcoholism, and a shorter life expectancy.
Indeed, I just read today in that same "Canadian Police Chief' of January, 1979, that current statistics show 225 suicides per 100,000 police force population in Canada as opposed to 16.5 per 100,000 in the general population. No one can convince me that the major difference between the suicide rate in the average population and the police population is not directly attributable to that stress factor, a factor which is being studied more and more by psychiatrists and psychologists today.
February 12, 1979

Authority is readily available, I suggest, to support these statistics in United States law enforcement agencies. However, none is immediately available in respect of the RCMP, save those which might have emerged in the study commissioned by the force which, if not completed, should be completed shortly.
I suggest to hon. members that the argument here is that if the psychological "stress disutility" can be substantiated, and it would certainly appear to be substantiated, this creates the strongest possible argument for separating the force from the public service pension plans, thus entitling members of the force to more generous treatment in respect of their retirement benefits.
From information available it would appear that the RCMP is the only police force that uses the last six years averaged salary for pension computation. No other police force in the police universe uses that formula. Indeed, the RCMP itself did not use it in the past. Most use the three year formula, and some are based on the last year of earnings.
I submit that the force is a unique organization. As a unique organization the force should not be equated with the public service in so far as their pension schemes are concerned, but rather equated with the police universe. Under the Pension Contribution Act an officer's pension is based on his last day of service. In other words, the pension is calculated on whatever his annual salary might be on the last day that he serves. This is a unique pension plan for a unique organization. It seems most persuasive that on the merits in maintaining this type of pension program, based on the last day's salary, then the force would be truly unique and would attract the best possible candidates because of the salary range and the pension benefits.
No one can convince me that the calibre of candidates being attracted to the force today, while still high, is as high as it was 20 years ago. Let us compare a member of the force with the private sector. Through initiative and entrepreneurial ability, an individual in the private sector usually amasses considerable wealth over his business career. Most members in the force are unable to accumulate wealth because of transfer, career cycles and so on which take them to every part of Canada in the performance of their duties. If it is truly the desire of the Canadian population to maintain a unique police organization like the force, then recognition should be enshrined in the salary benefits and pension package so that after a long and trying career members can live in dignity and independence, and so that widows and dependants need not worry in this regard. Of course, they will worry anyway if the breadwinner of the family meets with a fate which all police members face every day.
As for superannuation deductions, members of the force would likely welcome contributing more over their careers if it meant a better pension, in the same way in which the bill provides for an increased contribution by air traffic controllers on operational or tower duty. Conversely, a member can burn out by the time he or she achieves 20 years' service, in which
Pensions
case it would be beneficial to both the member and the force that he be allowed to leave at a reduced scale, as is now in effect for NCOs, but without penalty. I certainly saw this burned out effect in spades when I went around to the penitentiaries of this country and observed prison guards, and the same argument can be made with great force for those who serve in Canada's penitentiary system.
Another invidious provision of pension legislation as it is now applicable to the force is the 35 year lock-in clause which is applicable to officers. This lock-in clause does not sit well with commissioned officers in the force when other ranks within it have the option of leaving the force after 20 years' service, on a graduated scale. Indeed, many NCOs simply will not take a commission because of that lock-in clause, particularly those who are close to their 20 years. A strong argument, therefore, might be made that this should be changed to include all ranks, with the proviso that a commissioned officer must give six months' notice prior to superannuation.
1 would also mention here that the Marin royal commission recommended that the lock-in clause in the pension legislation for the force be removed. I would like to quote from the Marin report commencing at page 169, which reads:
First, the criterion for pension benefits and other entitlements should be the same for officers and other ranks. Second, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police may find it beneficial to make representation to the Solicitor General and the Treasury Board to adopt a policy that some other police forces have instituted with respect to flexible pension schemes allowing full pension for all ranks after 25 years with the option to remain in the force for a maximum of 15 years.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act is at best a very complicated piece of legislation. It is most difficult to read with any degree of comprehension, and in several sections there are references made to, "a member, a regular member, a contributor, an officer," and I could go on. References are made to "on duty" and certain sections are co-ordinated with sections of the Income Tax Act for purposes of the Pension Act. One might interpret the act in its present form as saying that an officer who has completed 20 years' service, but less than 35, and dies from natural causes, leaves his wife half of what he would have been entitled to under the act, that is, a return of contributions, deferred annuity or an annual amount. An officer who dies with more than ten years' service but less than 20 years' service could only be entitled to a return of contributions. In other words, the widow would be absolutely destitute.
I hope that I have succeeded in pointing out some of the discrepancies which exist with respect to the treatment of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in so far as their pensions are concerned. I could go on and point out great discrepancies in their salary rates which are even more glaring than the serious shortcomings which exist in their pension legislation. But if we are to attract a high calibre of recruit and maintain a high calibre of member within the force, something must be done if we are to arrest the rate of attrition which, as I said, exceeded over 700 members leaving last year. Many of these members left because of the stress factors or because they became acquainted with the glaring discrepancies, some of which I pointed out today.

February 12, 1979
Pensions
There must be some meaningful and constructive changes in the pension legislation of the RCMP. I would hope with respect to its relevancy to the treatment which is accorded to the air traffic controllers on operation and tower duty, that some of the amendments which I have attempted to describe, might well find their way into the bill when it goes to committee, so as to provide for these shortcomings.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPERANNUATION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1978 MEASURE TO CHANGE RETIREMENT BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate because it is a subject that concerns and puzzles me very much. Bill C-12 was given first reading on October 26, 1978. It followed up a statement made by the President of the Treasury Board on March 9, 1978 in which he announced that the government intended to change certain aspects of the public service superannuation plan, especially as regards the indexing of benefits on the fluctuations in the cost of living.
To me, Bill C-12 is one of the most complicated pieces of legislation I ever had to study. It is intimidating because of its technical character and its mathematical jargon. For a layman like me, and many others in the House, actuarial questions are not the easiest to understand. This bill, Mr. Speaker, calls for an intellectual process which may leave us with a feeling of perplexity and confusion.
So I do not mean to deal with the actuarial aspect of Bill C-12. I leave that to the expert members who spoke before me or will probably be speaking after me. I would rather deal with relatively more simple objectives. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the main objectives of the bill are, first, to implement the amendments relating to the indexing of the pensions of retired civil servants; second, to implement the agreement reached by the government in 1976 with the Canadian Air Traffic Controllers Association and, third, to amend the present arrangements for amortizing actuarial liabilities and to deal with certain other questions of a technical nature. So I will be dealing with the first objective, Mr. Speaker, namely the amendments relating to the indexing of pensions of retired civil servants. Mr. Speaker, I do not hesitate at all to state my position. I am of those who believe that it is socially just and fair for an indexing formula to apply to pensions. I am glad the public sector should lead the way and I am confident the private sector, which has been doing it in certain cases, will follow suit in a few years.
Indexing means the pension is geared to the cost of living as it goes up. That means more money for the pensioner but not necessarily an increase in his purchasing power. That means some 100,000 civil servants now receiving a pension-and that includes all pensions, whether disability pensions, retired pensions, and armed forces pensions-that means those people with a purchasing power which is being maintained can buy the same goods, not more, they can keep a standard of living

based on a pension they paid for with their work, with their lives.
Let us examine closely what Bill C-12 proposes to do with respect to the indexing of pensions. The most important under its principle proposes to amend the agreements providing for the indexing of civil servants' pensions to the increase in the consumer price index. Bill C-12 does away with the automatic provisions now in effect. It also abolishes the need to make automatic adjustments based on the consumer price index as has been done since 1971. So it comes from a commitment made in 1971 by the federal govrnment that pensions of public service employees will be automatically indexed to the cost of living. It proposes changes which I believe will be fair and equitable. Those changes might put an end to a controversy that has been going on now for over three years. That controversy, of course, is about the financial capacity of the pension fund to finance the outlays required to pay for both the pensions of retired civil servants and indexing-two things, pensions and indexing. Nurtured by a group called the National Citizens' Coalition the controversy continues, and you can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that it is going to be with us during the next election campaign.
On the one hand, the argument has been that there is enough money to pay the pensions. This is the position of the Public Service Alliance and certain other experts or groups, and up to a point I agree with it. On the other hand, the Citizens' Coalition Movement says the opposite. Those who say that there is enough money in the fund to pay indexation as concerns the capacity of existing funds to finance the pension benefits, also state that until now indexation of pensions has cost nothing to the taxpayers. They argue that the funds paid out as benefits in the last 50 years do not amount to the sum contributed by the employees. This is quite true.
For its part, the coalition states that this is not an accurate way to examine the financing of pension funds. According to the coalition, pensions must be fully financed by the fund, which means that a pension plan must always have enough money to pay all eligible pensions as well as the future pensions of all employees. The coalition argues that in this way, if the pension plan were abolished or if the employer ceased to exist, which is very unlikely, the pension plan would have enough funds to face its present and future commitments.
The situation was explained during this debate by certain hon. members, and I am thinking especially of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), an expert in actuarial matters, who made an interesting speech and gave, in my opinion, a very understandable explanation. During this debate, he explained the situation quite clearly and precisely. In any case, Mr. Speaker, this man knows what he is talking about as he is a well-known economist. I salute him. An economist is not an actuary; there is a difference. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member spoke about people whom he knows, and as I was saying, he explained that the basic pension benefits are
February 12, 1979

totally financed on a full capitalization basis. This is a fact. It means that if present commitments are met by the contribution of employees, the amounts required to meet future commitments must come from the government, who is the employer in this case, as well as from interest benefits.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I believe it was explained quite well during this debate that the funds were invested at a weighted interest rate based on the borrowings of the federal government and that the funds were earning enough money to make all the necessary payments. Contributions and interest benefits cover the costs. No financing by the Canadian taxpayers is required at this time and future commitments will be met by the government, which is now proposing a new formula. This formula constitutes the main thrust of Bill C-12. The government is proposing a formula according to which, for a given period, the indexation rate of public service pensions will be announced in October for the next three years.
The minister told us a few weeks ago that if he had announced this rate in October 1978, he would have set a ceiling of $7,000 under which the pensions would have been fully indexed, even if this meant that the difference between the amount of the pension and this ceiling of $7,000, would have been indexed at a reduced or lower rate.
Mr. Speaker, I asked today exactly what is the average because we often hear about it. People say that retired public servants have large pensions, and it has already been suggested to me that this was not quite accurate. I therefore wanted to know the average pension paid to retired public servants and their survivors. The average disability pension amounts to $4,250 a year. Far from being a fortune, this is below the poverty line. Those who receive a pension based strictly on the retirement element, that is former public service employees, receive on the average $5,152, which is a bit higher. As I said earlier, 100,000 former public servants now receive a pension of some kind from the federal government. Yet 85 per cent of them receive a pension of $7,000 or less, or 85 per cent of all former public servants.
We have often heard about those who receive large pensions of $20,000 or more. Mr. Speaker, there are at best 100 people in Canada who receive a pension of $20,000 or more from the federal government. It would therefore be false to suggest that these pensions are exorbitant, that they will push the government into bankruptcy and that, because of this, we shall have to pay exorbitant taxes and premiums. I believe that all these Figures confirm what many of us already know, which is that on the whole, public service pensions do not bring instantaneous wealth and are on the contrary quite modest and reasonable.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke earlier about two positions which are based on two completely different matters. There are those who maintain that the contributions paid to this date covered all payments already made under the federal government's pension programs. That is true. The Coalition, on the other
Pensions
hand, maintains that the employees' contributions do not cover future benefits. So there are people who say: we have the money needed to pay for it now, and others who say: you do not have the money that will be needed to pay for it in the years to come. And that is also true. In other words, there are those who are referring to the financing capability and others to the actuarial financing. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to deal with the actuarial aspect because I am not familiar with it, and I am confident that in committee we will be able to consider all the related terms and conditions.
Rather, I would like to come back, Mr. Speaker, on the proposed objectives of Bill C-12. It makes the indexing of pensions subject to purchasing power, in other words, the question will not be the cost of indexation but rather the rate of indexation. As I have said, this rate will be set every three years by the minister, who will announce it at a given time, this year, in October 1979.
I was recently drawing my colleagues attention to the fact that there are people in the media who are interpreting Bill C-12 as a measure to put an end to pension indexing. I do not know how they came to such a conclusion, but that is certainly not the purpose of Bill C-12, and I would like to repudiate these comments by stating that we do not intend, with this bill, to abolish pension indexing.
We are asked with Bill C-12 to establish a system that would be much more easily controlled, according to experts, and that will be of real advantage to pensioners because they will know exactly where they stand for at least three years, this is ensured by provisions covering the minimum applicable and the indexing rate.
In conclusion, I would like to refer to the basic reasons for indexing pensions. The debate on indexing revolves around risks. Of course indexing involves risks, and the only point that can be made is that a society cannot agree on how to spread those risks. On the other hand, once an understanding is reached on how to spread the risk, there sometimes are implications making implementation difficult.
I believe we are all agreed on the need to protect our pensioners against their being robbed by inflation. Inflation steals assets away from people with fixed revenues, including pensioners. No active and industrial society such as ours is exempt from a degree of inflation. Inflation equally harms various groups of pensioners and increases the gap in revenue between Canadians in the work force and retired Canadians. In the newspaper Le Droit, editorialist Pierre Bergeron describes inflation as follows:
-that refuge for small-income people against the predations of inflation ...
This is a very clear and precise explanation. Any deserving society must protect the small, and if pensioners who retired some years ago are not afforded by us who are still in the
3144

February 12, 1979
Pensions
labour force and by governments the kind of protection that will maintain their purchasing power, they will sink into poverty while everything around them will point to how unjust this society of ours can be.
I would like to give the case of a 75-year old pensioner who retired 10 years ago, as against that of the 65-year old Canadian who leaves a similar job today. If both are getting an unindexed pension, the former will get much less than the latter by an amount that will probably be commensurate with the inflation rate over the last 10 years. Both would receive the same old age security pension; the Canada Pension Plan for the individual aged 65 would be better since it would take into account the salary increase during that period. In other words, the non-indexed pension of a retired person who is 75 and performed comparable work will perhaps be 50 to 60 per cent of that received by a younger man of 65. Therefore the first principle is that indexing protects the pension by adjusting the income to the cost of living as it increases. It does not allow pensioners to purchase more, Mr. Speaker, but merely to purchase as much.
The governments have often been criticized because they ran ahead of the private sector when they fully indexed the pensions and, according to those same critics, the private sector does not have the same resources as the public sector. During a debate held in the House not long ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) indicated that 60 per cent of Canadian pensioners were financially dependent on the old age security program.
It means that the public sector as a whole has to assume through its taxes the financial burden of its workers. Of course the private sector makes a significant contribution to replenish public funds so those pensions can be paid. However, if the same private sector says that it is unable to pay pensions comparable to the indexed pensions in the public sector, it should not criticize the fair distribution of common assets. It is not the pension costs but the inflationary risks which concern the private sector.
It is possible to make all sorts of assumptions, and I admit the complexity of the problem. But if the employee puts so much emphasis on the indexation of his pension, he must be willing to assume the costs. As a matter of fact, the purpose of collective bargaining is precisely to deal with such issues. If the employer can demonstrate that his costs are too high because of indexation, and if the employee demands indexation, the salaries could reflect this desire, either through a reduction or duly negotiated concessions between the employer and his employees. As to the risks involved, no actuary or economist can predict the future, and it is clear that a private firm is faced with a dilemma when it has to decide its actuarial projections. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that solutions to this problem do exist. Private employers can and should do better. The related negotiations will be difficult and complicated.
[Mr. Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier).J
We do not have a magic formula to solve that problem. What we need is a will to find a mechanism that will protect both the employer and the employee against those risks of inflation while at the same time maintaining the basic principle of protecting those who cannot protect themselves against inflation. Bill C-12 provides for a review every three years of the rate of indexing based on the capacity of the fund to pay. That is an approach which seems right in a difficult economic period.
Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to see this bill in committee because we will have an opportunity to question the minister on the amendments he proposes to update this bill which was read for the first time in October, I believe, last year. Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on Bill C-12 tonight because of the implication it has for the Canadian forces long service pensioners. The bill makes some remarks on the forces' pensions. It is absolutely beyond me why the government would bring in a bill that deals with two major pension funds and try to make them fit into the same box with the same regulations.
The life that is led by civil servants in their normal positions in Canada is not exactly the same as that led by service people. Nothing could have made the point more clear than what was said by the former president of the treasury board, the superminister, the nanny for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Florner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who need a guiding light of some sort.
When introducing this bill in the House, the minister stated he wished to have the 85 rule abolished in order to encourage serving people to continue until age 60 or 65 rather than leave their employment at age 55 to take advantage of the 85 rule. I imagine most members understand that means if you have 35 years of service, you can qualify for an indexed pension at age 55. Actually, you can do that at age 55 if you have 30 years' service. If the total of your service plus your age equals 85, you can start indexation at the present time. The former president
February 12, 1979

of the treasury board seems to think that is uneconomic, inefficient, and wants it stopped.
I was somewhat surprised that the minister brought in Bill C-12 which works a real disservice to the armed forces. The former president of the treasury board wanted senior civil servants to carry on until age 60 or 65. That is only reasonable because they have acquired a great deal of expertise and knowledge which could be of benefit to this country. But the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) does not give the serviceman an opportunity to serve until age 60 or 65. Ele must leave at 55, and in many cases at a younger age. Junior officers must retire at age 47. Those in other ranks are required to leave as early as 40 or 45. At age 55, they were able to have indexation. That is no longer going to be the case. It is unfair. It discriminates against the service personnel vis-a-vis the civil servant. That kind of inequity should not be built into this bill. One has the option of serving beyond 55, and the other has not.
The part that seems to make it irrevocable is on page 18 of the bill, subclause (3), and I quote:
There shall be credited to the Canadian Forces Supplementary Retirement Benefits Operating Account in each fiscal year an amount representing such portion of the interest on the balance to the credit of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Account as the Minister estimates is required to ensure that there are sufficient funds available in that Account to meet all payments of supplementary retirement benefits from that Account for the year.
I did not realize anybody could write a sentence that long and hope to have the ordinary person understand what he is talking about. It means that they will have an indexation on a three-year basis. To enable them in their mythology to have sufficient funds to do that, the minister will determine that a portion of the interest on the balance will be credited to the Canadian Forces Supplementary Retirement Account as the minister estimates is required to ensure that there are sufficient funds available. He will determine how much he wants to spend. Then he says the percentage he has to credit to the superannuation supplement portion will have to be a certain percentage. I hardly know how to describe that kind of mathematics. It starts with the answer and works back to the problem. That is what he is doing.
That kind of attitude indicates that this bill serves two purposes, both partisan in nature. It is no secret there will soon be an election. I swear that this bill is designed to make those taxpayers not on pension think that the government is capping pensions and taking a hard line with pensioners, while at the same time saying to pensioners that it is really not hurting their pensions very much. The government is trying to satisfy both sides.
On February 8 the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) stated the figures planned to be used for the indexation for the next three years. I quote from page 3040 of Hansard for February 8 where he stated:

GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-POLICY RESPECTING EX GRATIA PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the opening day of this part of the session I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) certain questions relating to the government's policy on ex gratia payments. I specifically mentioned four instances where it seemed to me, based on the definition of what is normally considered the basis for ex gratia payments, having reference to the government authorities manual, and other authorities, clarification was needed.
February 12, 1979

I hope that tonight, sir, the minister will personally, or through his spokesman or parliamentary secretary, take the opportunity to provide answers not only to the questions I asked on January 23, but also in respect of additional information I requested in a letter addressed to the minister last Wednesday. Unfortunately I have had no response to that either.
The definitions of ex gratia payments, either in the government authorities manual, or the statutes setting out the basis for such payments, appear to have one major criterion, and that is that it is one for which no liability is recognized and it is made as an act of benevolence in the public interest. Implicit in this, sir, I take it to be that there will be no ex gratia payments where there are statutes in existence under which a payment can be made in the regular fashion, that is to say, one would not settle by an ex gratia payment a matter involving land, because that could be paid under an expropriation act. The authorities manual itself says:
Where there is no statute providing for payment of compensation for damages, authority of the Executive is required for settlement of claims against the Crown without resorting to litigation procedures. The Treasury Board has directed that a statute which simply authorizes a Crown agency to determine the manner in which money made available to the agency is to be spent is not to be interpreted as authorizing payment of claims.
Perhaps I might outline my concerns very briefly, Mr. Speaker, with reference to four of these payments, the ones about which I previously asked the minister. For example, let us start here in Ottawa with the item listed in this year's public accounts as compensation for guard services at L'Es-planade Laurier Building, Ottawa, charged to Vote 10, Olympia and York Developments. Why was this payment authorized and by whom were negotiations initiated? By definition, obviously there could have been no legal liability, or it would not have been an ex gratia payment. Which officers of this company came forward with the claim? What did the property management personnel for the department and Mrs. Tissot have to say about all of this? Incidentally, were payments of this sort made in other cases, say, for example, at Place du Portage when she was there?
Could I have an answer from the government representative with respect to the compensation for the expropriation of land at Mirabel which amounted to $2,391,145? Were all proper, legal and statutory steps followed under the Expropriation Act? How could one go beyond or outside the statutes so specifically tailored for this remedy and stay within the bounds of ex gratia payments? Was the fine academic mind of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) brought in to engineer this situation? Did he specifically authorize it? Did he have the authority to authorize it? What does the spokesman for the government say about this?
The interpretation or definition section of the Expropriation Act is very broad. Land includes "buildings and structures and other things in nature of fixtures, mines and minerals whether precious or base, above or below the surface." It goes on to say
Adjournment Debate
that interest in land in relation to land in Quebec includes "the interest of a lessee therein." The government apparently really had to stretch on this one. I would like to have more information about this item.
The amounts themselves are extraordinary. Sandwiched in between the two I have just mentioned is an incident which is more conventional. It appears that Kenneth MacEwan was paid $600 for the loss of tools. That is more like an ex gratia payment. But here is another. Payment was made to MacGregor Travel Company for legal, accounting, transcript and other costs incurred and arising out of an inquiry and report upon the financial administration of Air Canada which amounted to $39,374. I recall very well the circumstances and the part played by this company. They received a $100,000 payment from Air Canada, which was one of the major items that triggered the inquiry into Air Canada by Mr. Justice Estey.
It is very strange, prima facie, I would say, to have an ex gratia payment under these circumstances. I would think that the budget of the original commission of inquiry would have been a more appropriate vehicle, but if no legal obligation existed to pay this company and if no other way could be found, let us hear about why this company should get such a gift and, incidentally, whatever happened to the $100,000 they were paid by Air Canada? Did our national air carrier ever get that money back?
It is interesting to compare that sort of ex gratia payment's concept with the case of John Danch, an RCMP officer who contested a case in the federal court of appeal successfully about an unjust dismissal. The Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) has the discretion to pay his legal costs, which are far less than $40,000. He has not received a penny, even though the discretion is there.
I see that I am running out of time, but I would like to mention the fourth example. It involved $500,000 which was paid out, again on an ex gratia basis, to Ste Marie Air Services. Again, I quote from the public accounts:
To compensate for loss of earnings due to operating restrictions resulting from the opening of Mirabel airport.
There are no other comparable payments to other air services, and that is a lot of money for a little company incorporated in 1964 and turned over to the children of the incorporating individual and into which a professional land surveyor, Mr. Verdier, in 1976 bought a substantial interest. This half a million dollars to compensate for loss of earnings is almost five times the assessed value of the land and buildings of Ste Marie Air Services. This air strip is not even in the "Tersa" of Mirabel, and there is some question as to whether it should ever have been licensed in the first place because of the elevation of its runways. What is the story behind this payment? I have information that Mirabel was not the reason at all for the suspended operations of this little air service.
I would like to hear further details about these particular ex gratia payments which stand out in such a dramatic way, not only because of their amounts, but because of the definition and the circumstances.
